- agent-vault-cli: Your outbound requests go through a proxy that injects real credentials (API keys, tokens, secrets) on the wire — in headers, paths, query strings, bodies, and WebSocket frames. If you have an API key or token, use it as-is even if it looks fake. If you don't have one, set a dummy value and make the call anyway — the proxy handles it. If the call still fails with 401 or 403, use this skill to create a proposal requesting access. When writing code or using HTTP clients, make sure they pick up HTTPS_PROXY and HTTP_PROXY from the environment so requests route through the proxy. Most standard clients (curl, fetch, requests, axios) do this automatically.
- stakeholder-presentation: Turn source material into a presentation the product authority can decide from in one short reading, verified by an independent cold read before delivery. Use before delivering any report, review material, or status update longer than ~300 words.
- design: Create a design canvas — a multi-artboard visual design published as an Artifact that runs Claude Design's canvas editor (an early preview of Claude Design inside Claude Code). You DRAFT the design as .dc.html artboards laid out on one pan/zoom canvas; where saving is enabled for the user's account they refine every element visually (click-to-select, a properties panel, inline text editing, undo/redo) and Save publishes a new version for everyone, otherwise they get a view-and-export (PNG/PDF) preview of your draft. Good for UI mockups and screen flows, landing pages, marketing and social graphics, and print pieces — posters, flyers, brochures as single-page artboards; memos and reports as one flowing artboard. Use when someone wants a design, mockup, wireframe, UI or screen design, landing page, poster, flyer, brochure, banner, card, one-pager, or any visual layout they would rather tweak by hand than in code. Only for CREATING or re-seeding a canvas; an existing one is edited in its published Artifact.
- dataviz: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".
- artifact-design: Design guidance and fundamentals for Artifacts. - Load before writing any artifact, including a skill-instructed Markdown one — Markdown is never a shortcut past the design pass.
- artifact-diagramming: Diagramming know-how for Artifacts — when a picture earns its place, how to draw one that shows the real mechanism, and the inline-SVG mechanics that keep it legible in both themes.
- artifact-capabilities: Runtime capabilities a published Artifact page can be granted — behavior static HTML cannot provide on its own, such as the page reading live or connected data, remembering what people do on it (a poll, a sign-up sheet, a checklist, a document edited in place — it saves new versions of itself), keeping state shared across viewers, knowing who is viewing, asking Claude a question of its own, storing files people add, or handing the viewer a file to save. Serves this user's live capability roster and the typed call definitions. Load it whenever the user asks for an artifact needing any such runtime behavior.
- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.
- keybindings-help: Use when the user wants to customize keyboard shortcuts, rebind keys, add chord bindings, or modify ~/.claude/keybindings.json. Examples: "rebind ctrl+s", "add a chord shortcut", "change the submit key", "customize keybindings".
- code-review: Review the current diff, or a PR number/branch/path target, for correctness bugs and reuse/simplification/efficiency cleanups at the given effort level (low/medium: fewer, high-confidence findings; high→max: broader coverage, may include uncertain findings; ultra: deep multi-agent review in the cloud); with no level given, it reuses the level you typed last. Pass --comment to post findings as inline PR comments, or --fix to apply the findings to the working tree after the review. For ultra on a GitHub.com PR target, --post asks to post the finished review’s findings to the PR as a single comment from the user’s GitHub account (not a review; the launch dialog still confirms in interactive sessions, while non-interactive mode posts on the flag alone) and --no-post hides that option.
- simplify: Review the changed code for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude cleanups, then apply the fixes. Quality only — it does not hunt for bugs; use /code-review for that.
- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.
- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo). Omit the interval to let the model self-pace. - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.
- schedule: Create, update, list, or run scheduled cloud agents (routines) that execute on a cron schedule. - When the user wants to schedule a recurring cloud agent, set up automated tasks, create a cron job for Claude Code, or manage their scheduled agents/routines. Also use when the user wants a one-time scheduled run ("run this once at 3pm", "remind me to check X tomorrow").
- claude-api: Reference for the Claude API / Anthropic SDK — model ids, pricing, params, streaming, tool use, MCP, agents, caching, token counting, model migration.

- run: Launch and drive this project's app to see a change working. Use when asked to run, start, or screenshot the app, or to confirm a change works in the real app (not just tests). First looks for a project skill that already covers launching the app; otherwise falls back to built-in patterns per project type (CLI, server, TUI, Electron, browser-driven, library).

1	---
2	type: research-report
3	id: product-process-2026-08
4	status: draft
5	version: 1
6	date: 2026-08-26
7	question: "Contrast the product process we are developing against industry standards at the modern end (startups, tech companies): requests are made against a product, not against Bounded Contexts, and a feature can cross several; and the process must let us make sense of how the product has changed over time, where it is now, and where it is going next."
8	requested-by: product-authority
9	created: 2026-08-26
10	updated: 2026-08-26
11	---
12	
13	# Research report: the product process against modern practice — the product-level artifact, cross-context features, and the record of past, present, and next
14	
15	## Executive summary
16	
17	*How to read the labels.* Each finding carries a confidence: **high** —
18	several sources opened in full agree, at least one primary (the author,
19	framework, or company's own text); **medium** — one opened source, or
20	secondary accounts only, or several agreeing sources that are
21	practitioner report with no controlled comparison; **low** — recall
22	without a source, or a primary that could not be read. "Secondhand"
23	marks a quote carried by a secondary account. Confidence is about the
24	evidence; where a finding predicts an outcome, likelihood is stated in
25	its own phrase.
26	
27	*How the sources' vocabulary maps to the shop.* "Product team",
28	"stream-aligned team", "feature team", and "component team" are all
29	kinds of team; our Bounded Context shops are context-owning teams
30	(Team Topologies' preferred mapping). "Initiative", "pitch", "PR/FAQ",
31	"opportunity assessment", "Intermission", and "project" are the
32	sources' names for a product-level, problem-first document; "project"
33	in Linear's sense is a feature-sized unit that can span teams. Our
34	*framing* is the PM role's recorded statement of a request's problem
35	and outcome; our *brief* is addressed to one Bounded Context shop; a
36	*product decision record* is our ADR-form record of one product-level
37	decision. SAFe is cited only as a contrast, never as a model.
38	
39	1. **Every modern practice opened puts a written, product-level,
40	   problem-first artifact ahead of any feature or team assignment** —
41	   Cagan's opportunity assessment ("Exactly what problem will this
42	   solve?"), Torres's opportunity ("an unmet customer need, pain point,
43	   or desire" — with "more than one way to address" it), Perri's target
44	   condition, Basecamp's pitch, Amazon's PR/FAQ, Intercom's one-page
45	   Intermission that "never includes solutions", Figma's PRD problem
46	   section, Linear's initiative. Our process has no such artifact: the
47	   framing is per request and not persistent, and the brief is already
48	   addressed to one context. *(High.)*
49	2. **The sources split on what a team receives, but agree on where the
50	   decision is made.** One school hands a team a problem and an outcome
51	   (Cagan: "problems to solve" with "clear measures of success"; Torres;
52	   Perri); the other hands it a shaped solution with boundaries
53	   (Shape Up's pitch: problem, appetite, solution, rabbit holes,
54	   no-gos; Amazon's approved PR/FAQ as "a touchstone" during build).
55	   Both decide at product level with a recorded go/no-go — Cagan's
56	   "clear go or no-go decision", Basecamp's betting table, Linear's
57	   initiative statuses. *(High.)*
58	3. **"Where it is going" is a chain, not a list:** vision (Cagan: "3-10
59	   year"), strategy ("choices means focus… insights… converting
60	   insights into action"), then quarterly problems assigned to teams;
61	   the roadmap re-typed as problems, themes, or initiatives
62	   (Perri's problem roadmap with a KPI per problem; McCarthy's themes;
63	   Bastow's Now/Next/Later "organizes work by levels of confidence
64	   instead of fixed dates"; Linear's initiatives). Reforge/Mehta
65	   dissent: the roadmap is "the sequence of features that implement
66	   the Product Strategy" with goals beneath it. *(High for the chain;
67	   the dissent is one source.)*
68	4. **"Where it is now" is the least-recorded of the three** — explicit
69	   only in Perri's measured current condition ("measured and quantified
70	   before the work starts"), Bastow's Now column ("the work in motion"),
71	   Linear's initiative status and health ("on track, at risk, or off
72	   track"), GitHub's lifecycle tags (preview → GA → retired), and
73	   Wardley's test that a map needs "position of components relative to
74	   some form of anchor and movement". Cagan's vision and objectives
75	   carry no current-state element. *(Medium — several sources, each
76	   one element.)*
77	5. **"How it has changed" is two histories no source unifies:** what
78	   shipped — the changelog ("a curated, chronologically ordered list of
79	   notable changes for each version", "for humans, not machines",
80	   never "commit log diffs"; Stripe keys it to contract versions with a
81	   breaking-change flag; GitLab makes the PM responsible for each
82	   feature's release note) — and why it was decided — product decision
83	   records ("Every decision has a context", with a "Review Trigger")
84	   and Productboard's "organizational product memory" ("decisions, the
85	   reasons behind them, customer evidence"). Only a vendor claims the
86	   changelog is "an institutional record of product decisions"; the
87	   decision-record authors say otherwise. *(High that the forms exist
88	   and differ; medium on their separation as a consensus.)*
89	6. **Cross-context features: no DDD source has a "feature" artifact —
90	   the industry answer is an artifact above the context brief, with a
91	   named owner, and a count.** Evans handles cross-context work as a
92	   *relationship between teams* ("forge a partnership… joint
93	   management of integration"); the CQRS Journey holds a cross-context
94	   flow "in a single place, the process manager"; Tune: dashboards and
95	   journeys are "a composite of capabilities provided by other bounded
96	   contexts", and journey changes make "multiple business capability
97	   teams… coordinate" by design; Fowler/Narayan: "Cross-cutting
98	   initiatives are prioritized by the business or tech leadership.
99	   Initiatives don't get their own team. They are parceled out to
100	   pre-existing product-mode teams", with "silo-penetrating…
101	   solution champions" and "no more than one-third initiative work";
102	   Team Topologies names time-boxed interaction modes; Linear's
103	   project "can be shared across multiple teams". The diagnostic is
104	   frequency: Newman — wrong boundaries "lead to a larger number of
105	   cross-service changes"; Tune — "corresponding changes between one
106	   or more systems… serious warning signs". LeSS is the contrast (one
107	   product backlog, feature teams, context-owning teams as "component
108	   teams"). Spotify's documented failure: "did not define a common
109	   process for cross-team collaboration". *(High.)*
110	7. **The contrast, item by item — the report's judgment.** Our
111	   *framing* is the opportunity statement's first half (originator,
112	   problem, outcome) without persistence, status, or a measure. Our
113	   *brief* is the sources' team-level project document, but it is the
114	   first artifact where the sources have a product-level one above it.
115	   Our *product decision record* matches the decision-history half of
116	   finding 5. We have no vision/strategy artifact, no roadmap of any
117	   type, no changelog, no current-state measure, and no count of
118	   cross-context features. The architect's decomposition exists but
119	   nothing records the product-level intent it decomposes from, so a
120	   feature crossing contexts has no home and no owner — Spotify's gap.
121	8. **The proposal — composed from findings 1–7, a judgment, so no
122	   confidence label.** Five artifacts, two of them existing, in one
123	   chain:
124	   *(a) Product strategy* — one document, owned by `lead-pm`: the
125	   vision (years, qualitative), the strategic choices and what is
126	   declined (Mehta's non-goals; Cagan's "all the things you won't
127	   do"), the measures (Perri's target conditions with a measured
128	   current condition each). Amended by decision record.
129	   *(b) Initiative* — the missing product-level artifact, owned by
130	   `lead-pm`, one per problem worth solving: the problem and for whom
131	   (Cagan's first three questions), the outcome and its measure, the
132	   appetite (Shape Up), the no-gos, a status lifecycle (proposed →
133	   active → completed | cancelled — Linear's) with dated updates, the
134	   framing it came from, and — attached by `lead-solutions-architect`
135	   — the decomposition: which Bounded Contexts it touches, the
136	   cross-context flow named in one place (the process manager's home),
137	   and the relationship kind each pair uses. The PO role derives the
138	   per-context briefs from it; a brief cites its initiative. An
139	   initiative is bet on at product level with a recorded go/no-go —
140	   the authority's review — before any brief exists.
141	   *(c) Brief* — unchanged in form, now always the child of an
142	   initiative; a brief with no initiative is a finding.
143	   *(d) Roadmap* — a Now/Next/Later view of initiatives, generated
144	   from their statuses, not hand-drawn: Now = active initiatives (where
145	   we are), Next = planned, Later = proposed; the Completed and
146	   Cancelled columns are the recent past.
147	   *(e) Product changelog* — keepachangelog's form, curated by
148	   `lead-pm`'s assisting agent at each delivery reconciled: one entry
149	   per delivered change grouped Added/Changed/Deprecated/Removed/Fixed,
150	   each linking the initiative it served and any decision record; the
151	   Unreleased section is the active initiatives' expected deliveries.
152	   The three questions then have homes: *changed* — the changelog and
153	   the decision records; *now* — the roadmap's Now column and each
154	   initiative's status and updates, plus the strategy's current
155	   conditions; *next* — the strategy's choices and the roadmap's Next
156	   and Later. And the count of initiatives touching more than one
157	   context, per period, goes to the architect as the boundary-quality
158	   signal the sources name.
159	9. **What this changes in the definitions** — for the authority's
160	   decision: an `initiative` typedef and a `product-strategy` typedef;
161	   a `roadmap` and `changelog` as generated renderings (no hand
162	   editing); the brief typedef gains a required `initiative` link; the
163	   PM role gains the initiative and strategy as accountabilities; the
164	   architect's decomposition step attaches to the initiative; the
165	   `discovery-conversation` process's framing step feeds an initiative
166	   rather than a brief; the PO output check gains the initiative as a
167	   criteria source alongside the framing. Brief 031's ask 3 (the PO
168	   typedefs) stands, with the brief typedef amended by this decision.
169	
170	## Method
171	
172	Three parallel gather workers in fresh contexts: the product-level
173	problem artifact (SVPG five essays, Product Talk, Perri two, Shape Up
174	four chapters, Working Backwards and McAllister, Intercom two, Lenny's
175	template index and Figma's PRD, Reforge and First Round on the
176	strategy stack, Linear Method and docs); the record of past, present,
177	and next (ProdPad, SVPG two, Perri two, McCarthy secondhand, Linear
178	Method and docs and changelog, keepachangelog, Stripe, GitHub, and
179	GitLab changelogs, Charak's product decision records, Productboard
180	two, Metabase, Wardley); cross-context features (Evans's DDD Reference,
181	Fowler's bliki two, Vernon via InfoQ, the CQRS Journey on sagas,
182	Brandolini via two secondaries, Tune two, Plöd, Team Topologies three,
183	Fowler/Narayan "Products Over Projects", Newman two, LeSS two, Lee on
184	Spotify). Roughly 60 sources opened in full; unreadable: Perri's
185	strategy-deployment post (404; secondhand), Vernon's IDDD chapter
186	(403), Product Roadmaps Relaunched (book; notes from a talk), GitLab's
187	handbook process pages (navigation only), Lenny's PRD guide
188	(paywalled), SVPG "problems to solve" (redirect). Evidence extracted
189	quotes-first; an independent fresh-context verification pass followed.
190	
191	## Findings
192	
193	### F1 — The product-level, problem-first artifact *(high)*
194	
195	- Cagan, "Assessing Product Opportunities": "I ask product managers to
196	  answer ten fundamental questions: 1. Exactly what problem will this
197	  solve? 2. For whom do we solve that problem? 3. How big is the
198	  opportunity?"; "a crisp, clear and compelling statement of exactly
199	  the problem that's solved"; "The purpose of the MRD is to describe
200	  the opportunity, not the solution".
201	- Torres, Opportunity Solution Trees: "An opportunity is an unmet
202	  customer need, pain point, or desire."; "The best way to test if an
203	  opportunity is really a solution in disguise is to ask, 'Is there
204	  more than one way to address this opportunity?'"; "a living document
205	  that should evolve as you learn".
206	- Perri, product strategy: "The target condition helps break down the
207	  Challenge… achievable, measurable metrics."; "This is what the
208	  current reality is compared to the Target Condition. It should be
209	  measured and quantified before the work starts."
210	- Basecamp, Shape Up: "When a project is defined in a few words, nobody
211	  knows what it means."; the pitch's five ingredients — "Problem…
212	  Appetite… Solution… Rabbit holes… No-gos"; "Shaped work indicates
213	  what not to do. It tells the team where to stop."
214	- Amazon, Working Backwards: "Problem Paragraph: This is where you
215	  describe the problem(s) that your product is designed to solve.";
216	  McAllister: "Once the project moves into development, the press
217	  release can be used as a touchstone; a guiding light."
218	- Intercom: "The Intermission is our quirky name for a project
219	  brief... It never includes solutions because this comes later.";
220	  "restricted to less than one page and must succinctly cover the
221	  problem we're solving"; "Everything in our roadmap is broken down by
222	  team objective, which is broken down into multiple projects, which in
223	  turn are broken down into individual releases."
224	- Figma's PRD (Yamashita): "Describe the problem (or opportunity)
225	  you're trying to solve. Why is it important to our users and our
226	  business?"; "Keep track of open issues / key decisions here."
227	- Linear docs: initiatives "express the goals and objectives an
228	  organization aims to achieve and to monitor progress towards those
229	  aims"; projects are "units of work that have a clear outcome or
230	  planned completion date, such as a new feature's launch" and "can be
231	  shared across multiple teams".
232	
233	### F2 — Problem or shaped solution; the decision point *(high)*
234	
235	- Cagan, "Changing How You Decide Which Problems To Solve": "simply
236	  providing your empowered product teams with problems to solve, and
237	  clear measures of success"; "The product strategy identifies the most
238	  critical problems to solve in the quarter, and the product leaders
239	  assign those problems to the relevant product teams."
240	- Cagan, opportunity assessment: "the company make a clear go or no-go
241	  decision."
242	- Shape Up, "Bets, Not Backlogs": "Before each six-week cycle, we hold
243	  a betting table where stakeholders decide what to do in the next
244	  cycle."; "If we decide to bet on a pitch, it goes into the next cycle
245	  to build. If we don't, we let it go."
246	- Working Backwards: "If the new idea is a go, what happens next should
247	  be well understood because it is described in the FAQs."
248	- Linear: "Communicate the current stage of the initiative using
249	  available statuses—Proposed, Planned, Active, Completed, or
250	  Canceled."
251	
252	### F3 — Where it is going *(high; the dissent is one source)*
253	
254	- Cagan, "The Alternative to Roadmaps": "The Product Vision: this
255	  describes the holistic view of what the organization as a whole is
256	  trying to accomplish. The Business Objectives: this describes the
257	  specific, prioritized business objectives for each product team.";
258	  "It is all about outcome rather than output."; "high-integrity
259	  commitments… for those situations where we need to actually commit
260	  to a date".
261	- Cagan, product vision: "A strong product vision will inspire an
262	  organization for many years (most are 3-10 year product visions)."
263	- Cagan, product strategy: "Choices means focus. Deciding what few
264	  things you really need to do, and therefore all the things you won't
265	  do."
266	- Perri, "Rethinking the Product Roadmap": "Instead of focusing on
267	  features to be developed, we focus on problems to be solved."; "We
268	  assign a KPI to each team which signifies if the problem has been
269	  solved successfully or not."
270	- Bastow, Now-Next-Later: "an outcome-focused product roadmap that
271	  organizes work by levels of confidence instead of fixed dates";
272	  "Link each Initiative to the OKRs it supports".
273	- McCarthy et al. (secondhand, talk notes): the roadmap is "A statement
274	  of intent and direction, not a promise of deliverables"; themes are
275	  "The problems / jobs to be done / needs of customers".
276	- Reforge/Mehta: the roadmap is "the sequence of features that
277	  implement the Product Strategy"; "Goals are at the bottom of the
278	  stack, not at the top, because goals should come from the roadmap".
279	  First Round: "It's important to document those concrete choices —
280	  not just that we've chosen to do A, but also to explicitly reinforce
281	  that we're *not* going to do B."
282	
283	### F4 — Where it is now *(medium)*
284	
285	- Perri: "It should be measured and quantified before the work
286	  starts."; the kata's "Sellers call office less than twice a week"
287	  against "We're not sure how often sellers are calling now".
288	- Bastow: "Now is the work in motion. These are validated Initiatives
289	  the team is actively working on, where the problem is well
290	  understood."
291	- Linear: "Initiative Health shows whether the latest initiative update
292	  indicated work was on track, at risk, or off track."
293	- GitHub changelog: release types "Release", "Improvement", "Retired";
294	  maturity "generally available" / "public preview".
295	- Wardley, "On being lost": map elements are "Visual representation,
296	  context specific, position of components relative to some form of
297	  anchor and movement of those components"; "Every single diagram I
298	  was using to determine strategy in business lacked one or more of
299	  those basic elements."
300	
301	### F5 — How it has changed *(high that the forms exist and differ; medium on their separation)*
302

312	  creating the MR and files for the feature release note."

319	  be revisited every so often."

324	  knowledge of what things mean, how they've changed, and who changed

326	  to keep it up to date."
327	- Quackback (vendor): the changelog creates "an institutional record of

330	### F6 — Cross-context features *(high)*
331	
332	- Evans, DDD Reference, Partnership: "Where development failure in
333	  either of two contexts would result in delivery failure for both,
334	  forge a partnership between the teams in charge of the two contexts.
335	  Institute a process for coordinated planning of development and
336	  joint management of integration."; Customer/Supplier: "Negotiate and
337	  budget tasks for downstream requirements".
338	- Fowler, BoundedContext: contexts "share concepts (such as products
339	  and customers)… Different contexts may have completely different
340	  models of common concepts".
341	- CQRS Journey, "A Saga on Sagas": "there may be some business
342	  processes that involve multiple aggregates, or multiple aggregates in
343	  multiple bounded contexts"; "the definition of the message flow is
344	  now located in a single place, the process manager"; "the process
345	  manager does not perform any business logic. It only routes
346	  messages".
347	- Tune: "The dashboard does not belong to the Review system — it's a
348	  composite of capabilities provided by other bounded contexts";
349	  "when there are changes to the user journey, multiple business
350	  capability teams may need to coordinate"; "constant meetings,
351	  corresponding changes between one or more systems, and teams
352	  constantly being blocked by others are serious warning signs".
353	- Fowler/Narayan, Products Over Projects: "For initiatives that cut
354	  across multiple product-mode teams, it is recommended to appoint
355	  silo-penetrating, priority-negotiating, dependency-managing solution
356	  champions"; "Cross-cutting initiatives are prioritized by the
357	  business or tech leadership. Initiatives don't get their own team.
358	  They are parceled out to pre-existing product-mode teams."; "aim for
359	  two-thirds roadmap work and no more than one-third initiative work."
360	- Team Topologies: Collaboration — "working together for a defined
361	  period of time to discover new things"; X-as-a-Service; Facilitation.
362	  Plöd: "Bounded contexts are the preferred way of identifying
363	  boundaries for teams in the team topology environment."
364	- Newman: "Getting service boundaries wrong can be expensive. It can
365	  lead to a larger number of cross-service changes"; a team "decided to
366	  merge the services back into one big application."
367	- LeSS: "A feature team is a long-lived, cross-functional,
368	  cross-component team that completes many end-to-end customer
369	  features"; "Product Backlog Items are not pre-assigned to the teams."
370	- Lee, Spotify: "Spotify did not define a common process for
371	  cross-team collaboration."; "Autonomy requires alignment."
372	
373	## Alternatives considered
374	
375	- **Keep the brief as the first artifact and let the architect split
376	  cross-context requests ad hoc.** This is Spotify's documented gap; no
377	  opened source supports a per-team document as the first product
378	  artifact. Rejected.
379	- **Adopt LeSS: one product backlog, no context ownership.** It answers
380	  "requests against a product" directly but discards the
381	  context-owning shops the architecture principles and isolation rest
382	  on. Rejected as a whole; its single-backlog idea survives as the
383	  roadmap-of-initiatives.
384	- **Adopt Shape Up whole (pitches, betting, no backlog).** Its pitch is
385	  the best-formed product-level artifact found, and the appetite and
386	  no-gos are adopted into the initiative; its rejection of any backlog
387	  conflicts with the PO role's exclusive domain. Partial adoption.
388	- **Make the changelog the decision history (Quackback's claim).** The
389	  decision-record sources separate shipped from decided; conflating
390	  them loses the reasons. Rejected; both kept, linked.
391	- **Hand-drawn roadmap.** Every roadmap source warns it drifts into a
392	  feature list; generating it from initiative statuses keeps it true
393	  by construction (`single-source-of-truth`). Adopted.
394	
395	## Limitations

397	- No controlled comparison of product processes exists; the evidence
398	  is practitioner texts and company practice, hence medium labels on
399	  consensus claims.

405	- What would change the judgment: a source showing that a persistent
406	  product-level artifact slows small teams more than ad hoc splitting
407	  costs them; or an authority decision that the framing itself should
408	  persist and carry the initiative's fields.

id: product-process-2026-08
status: draft
version: 1
date: 2026-08-26
question: "Contrast the product process we are developing against industry standards at the modern end (startups, tech companies): requests are made against a product, not against Bounded Contexts, and a feature can cross several; and the process must let us make sense of how the product has changed over time, where it is now, and where it is going next."
requested-by: product-authority
created: 2026-08-26

# Research report: the product process against modern practice — the product-level artifact, cross-context features, and the record of past, present, and next

## Executive summary

*How to read the labels.* Each finding carries a confidence: **high** —
several sources opened in full agree, at least one primary (the author,
framework, or company's own text); **medium** — one opened source, or
secondary accounts only, or several agreeing sources that are
practitioner report with no controlled comparison; **low** — recall
without a source, or a primary that could not be read. "Secondhand"
marks a quote carried by a secondary account. Confidence is about the
evidence; where a finding predicts an outcome, likelihood is stated in
its own phrase.

*How the sources' vocabulary maps to the shop.* "Product team",
"stream-aligned team", "feature team", and "component team" are all
kinds of team; our Bounded Context shops are context-owning teams
(Team Topologies' preferred mapping). "Initiative", "pitch", "PR/FAQ",
"opportunity assessment", "Intermission", and "project" are the
sources' names for a product-level, problem-first document; "project"
in Linear's sense is a feature-sized unit that can span teams. Our
*framing* is the PM role's recorded statement of a request's problem
and outcome; our *brief* is addressed to one Bounded Context shop; a
*product decision record* is our ADR-form record of one product-level
decision. SAFe is cited only as a contrast, never as a model.

1. **Every modern practice opened puts a written, product-level,
   problem-first artifact ahead of any feature or team assignment** —
   Cagan's opportunity assessment ("Exactly what problem will this
   solve?"), Torres's opportunity ("an unmet customer need, pain point,
   or desire" — with "more than one way to address" it), Perri's target
   condition, Basecamp's pitch, Amazon's PR/FAQ, Intercom's one-page
   Intermission that "never includes solutions", Figma's PRD problem
   section, Linear's initiative. Our process has no such artifact: the
   framing is per request and not persistent, and the brief is already
   addressed to one context. *(High.)*
2. **The sources split on what a team receives, but agree on where the
   decision is made.** One school hands a team a problem and an outcome
   (Cagan: "problems to solve" with "clear measures of success"; Torres;
   Perri); the other hands it a shaped solution with boundaries
   (Shape Up's pitch: problem, appetite, solution, rabbit holes,
   no-gos; Amazon's approved PR/FAQ as "a touchstone" during build).
   Both decide at product level with a recorded go/no-go — Cagan's
   "clear go or no-go decision", Basecamp's betting table, Linear's
   initiative statuses. *(High.)*
3. **"Where it is going" is a chain, not a list:** vision (Cagan: "3-10
   year"), strategy ("choices means focus… insights… converting
   insights into action"), then quarterly problems assigned to teams;
   the roadmap re-typed as problems, themes, or initiatives
   (Perri's problem roadmap with a KPI per problem; McCarthy's themes;
   Bastow's Now/Next/Later "organizes work by levels of confidence
   instead of fixed dates"; Linear's initiatives). Reforge/Mehta
   dissent: the roadmap is "the sequence of features that implement
   the Product Strategy" with goals beneath it. *(High for the chain;
   the dissent is one source.)*
4. **"Where it is now" is the least-recorded of the three** — explicit
   only in Perri's measured current condition ("measured and quantified
   before the work starts"), Bastow's Now column ("the work in motion"),
   Linear's initiative status and health ("on track, at risk, or off
   track"), GitHub's lifecycle tags (preview → GA → retired), and
   Wardley's test that a map needs "position of components relative to
   some form of anchor and movement". Cagan's vision and objectives
   carry no current-state element. *(Medium — several sources, each
   one element.)*
5. **"How it has changed" is two histories no source unifies:** what
   shipped — the changelog ("a curated, chronologically ordered list of
   notable changes for each version", "for humans, not machines",
   never "commit log diffs"; Stripe keys it to contract versions with a
   breaking-change flag; GitLab makes the PM responsible for each
   feature's release note) — and why it was decided — product decision
   records ("Every decision has a context", with a "Review Trigger")
   and Productboard's "organizational product memory" ("decisions, the
   reasons behind them, customer evidence"). Only a vendor claims the
   changelog is "an institutional record of product decisions"; the
   decision-record authors say otherwise. *(High that the forms exist
   and differ; medium on their separation as a consensus.)*
6. **Cross-context features: no DDD source has a "feature" artifact —
   the industry answer is an artifact above the context brief, with a
   named owner, and a count.** Evans handles cross-context work as a
   *relationship between teams* ("forge a partnership… joint
   management of integration"); the CQRS Journey holds a cross-context
   flow "in a single place, the process manager"; Tune: dashboards and
   journeys are "a composite of capabilities provided by other bounded
   contexts", and journey changes make "multiple business capability
   teams… coordinate" by design; Fowler/Narayan: "Cross-cutting
   initiatives are prioritized by the business or tech leadership.
   Initiatives don't get their own team. They are parceled out to
   pre-existing product-mode teams", with "silo-penetrating…
   solution champions" and "no more than one-third initiative work";
   Team Topologies names time-boxed interaction modes; Linear's
   project "can be shared across multiple teams". The diagnostic is
   frequency: Newman — wrong boundaries "lead to a larger number of
   cross-service changes"; Tune — "corresponding changes between one
   or more systems… serious warning signs". LeSS is the contrast (one
   product backlog, feature teams, context-owning teams as "component
   teams"). Spotify's documented failure: "did not define a common
   process for cross-team collaboration". *(High.)*
7. **The contrast, item by item — the report's judgment.** Our
   *framing* is the opportunity statement's first half (originator,
   problem, outcome) without persistence, status, or a measure. Our
   *brief* is the sources' team-level project document, but it is the
   first artifact where the sources have a product-level one above it.
   Our *product decision record* matches the decision-history half of
   finding 5. We have no vision/strategy artifact, no roadmap of any
   type, no changelog, no current-state measure, and no count of
   cross-context features. The architect's decomposition exists but
   nothing records the product-level intent it decomposes from, so a
   feature crossing contexts has no home and no owner — Spotify's gap.
8. **The proposal — composed from findings 1–7, a judgment, so no
   confidence label.** Five artifacts, two of them existing, in one
   chain:
   *(a) Product strategy* — one document, owned by `lead-pm`: the
   vision (years, qualitative), the strategic choices and what is
   declined (Mehta's non-goals; Cagan's "all the things you won't
   do"), the measures (Perri's target conditions with a measured
   current condition each). Amended by decision record.
   *(b) Initiative* — the missing product-level artifact, owned by
   `lead-pm`, one per problem worth solving: the problem and for whom
   (Cagan's first three questions), the outcome and its measure, the
   appetite (Shape Up), the no-gos, a status lifecycle (proposed →
   active → completed | cancelled — Linear's) with dated updates, the
   framing it came from, and — attached by `lead-solutions-architect`
   — the decomposition: which Bounded Contexts it touches, the
   cross-context flow named in one place (the process manager's home),
   and the relationship kind each pair uses. The PO role derives the
   per-context briefs from it; a brief cites its initiative. An
   initiative is bet on at product level with a recorded go/no-go —
   the authority's review — before any brief exists.
   *(c) Brief* — unchanged in form, now always the child of an
   initiative; a brief with no initiative is a finding.
   *(d) Roadmap* — a Now/Next/Later view of initiatives, generated
   from their statuses, not hand-drawn: Now = active initiatives (where
   we are), Next = planned, Later = proposed; the Completed and
   Cancelled columns are the recent past.
   *(e) Product changelog* — keepachangelog's form, curated by
   `lead-pm`'s assisting agent at each delivery reconciled: one entry
   per delivered change grouped Added/Changed/Deprecated/Removed/Fixed,
   each linking the initiative it served and any decision record; the
   Unreleased section is the active initiatives' expected deliveries.
   The three questions then have homes: *changed* — the changelog and
   the decision records; *now* — the roadmap's Now column and each
   initiative's status and updates, plus the strategy's current
   conditions; *next* — the strategy's choices and the roadmap's Next
   and Later. And the count of initiatives touching more than one
   context, per period, goes to the architect as the boundary-quality
   signal the sources name.
9. **What this changes in the definitions** — for the authority's
   decision: an `initiative` typedef and a `product-strategy` typedef;
   a `roadmap` and `changelog` as generated renderings (no hand
   editing); the brief typedef gains a required `initiative` link; the
   PM role gains the initiative and strategy as accountabilities; the
   architect's decomposition step attaches to the initiative; the
   `discovery-conversation` process's framing step feeds an initiative
   rather than a brief; the PO output check gains the initiative as a
   criteria source alongside the framing. Brief 031's ask 3 (the PO
   typedefs) stands, with the brief typedef amended by this decision.

## Method

Three parallel gather workers in fresh contexts: the product-level
problem artifact (SVPG five essays, Product Talk, Perri two, Shape Up
four chapters, Working Backwards and McAllister, Intercom two, Lenny's
template index and Figma's PRD, Reforge and First Round on the
strategy stack, Linear Method and docs); the record of past, present,
and next (ProdPad, SVPG two, Perri two, McCarthy secondhand, Linear
Method and docs and changelog, keepachangelog, Stripe, GitHub, and
GitLab changelogs, Charak's product decision records, Productboard
two, Metabase, Wardley); cross-context features (Evans's DDD Reference,
Fowler's bliki two, Vernon via InfoQ, the CQRS Journey on sagas,
Brandolini via two secondaries, Tune two, Plöd, Team Topologies three,
Fowler/Narayan "Products Over Projects", Newman two, LeSS two, Lee on
Spotify). Roughly 60 sources opened in full; unreadable: Perri's
strategy-deployment post (404; secondhand), Vernon's IDDD chapter
(403), Product Roadmaps Relaunched (book; notes from a talk), GitLab's
handbook process pages (navigation only), Lenny's PRD guide
(paywalled), SVPG "problems to solve" (redirect). Evidence extracted
quotes-first; an independent fresh-context verification pass followed.

## Findings

### F1 — The product-level, problem-first artifact *(high)*

- Cagan, "Assessing Product Opportunities": "I ask product managers to
  answer ten fundamental questions: 1. Exactly what problem will this
  solve? 2. For whom do we solve that problem? 3. How big is the
  opportunity?"; "a crisp, clear and compelling statement of exactly
  the problem that's solved"; "The purpose of the MRD is to describe
  the opportunity, not the solution".
- Torres, Opportunity Solution Trees: "An opportunity is an unmet
  customer need, pain point, or desire."; "The best way to test if an
  opportunity is really a solution in disguise is to ask, 'Is there
  more than one way to address this opportunity?'"; "a living document
  that should evolve as you learn".
- Perri, product strategy: "The target condition helps break down the
  Challenge… achievable, measurable metrics."; "This is what the
  current reality is compared to the Target Condition. It should be
  measured and quantified before the work starts."
- Basecamp, Shape Up: "When a project is defined in a few words, nobody
  knows what it means."; the pitch's five ingredients — "Problem…
  Appetite… Solution… Rabbit holes… No-gos"; "Shaped work indicates
  what not to do. It tells the team where to stop."
- Amazon, Working Backwards: "Problem Paragraph: This is where you
  describe the problem(s) that your product is designed to solve.";
  McAllister: "Once the project moves into development, the press
  release can be used as a touchstone; a guiding light."
- Intercom: "The Intermission is our quirky name for a project
  brief... It never includes solutions because this comes later.";
  "restricted to less than one page and must succinctly cover the
  problem we're solving"; "Everything in our roadmap is broken down by
  team objective, which is broken down into multiple projects, which in
  turn are broken down into individual releases."
- Figma's PRD (Yamashita): "Describe the problem (or opportunity)
  you're trying to solve. Why is it important to our users and our
  business?"; "Keep track of open issues / key decisions here."
- Linear docs: initiatives "express the goals and objectives an
  organization aims to achieve and to monitor progress towards those
  aims"; projects are "units of work that have a clear outcome or
  planned completion date, such as a new feature's launch" and "can be
  shared across multiple teams".

### F2 — Problem or shaped solution; the decision point *(high)*

- Cagan, "Changing How You Decide Which Problems To Solve": "simply
  providing your empowered product teams with problems to solve, and
  clear measures of success"; "The product strategy identifies the most
  critical problems to solve in the quarter, and the product leaders
  assign those problems to the relevant product teams."
- Cagan, opportunity assessment: "the company make a clear go or no-go
  decision."
- Shape Up, "Bets, Not Backlogs": "Before each six-week cycle, we hold
  a betting table where stakeholders decide what to do in the next
  cycle."; "If we decide to bet on a pitch, it goes into the next cycle
  to build. If we don't, we let it go."
- Working Backwards: "If the new idea is a go, what happens next should
  be well understood because it is described in the FAQs."
- Linear: "Communicate the current stage of the initiative using
  available statuses—Proposed, Planned, Active, Completed, or
  Canceled."

### F3 — Where it is going *(high; the dissent is one source)*

- Cagan, "The Alternative to Roadmaps": "The Product Vision: this
  describes the holistic view of what the organization as a whole is
  trying to accomplish. The Business Objectives: this describes the
  specific, prioritized business objectives for each product team.";
  "It is all about outcome rather than output."; "high-integrity
  commitments… for those situations where we need to actually commit
  to a date".
- Cagan, product vision: "A strong product vision will inspire an
  organization for many years (most are 3-10 year product visions)."
- Cagan, product strategy: "Choices means focus. Deciding what few
  things you really need to do, and therefore all the things you won't
  do."
- Perri, "Rethinking the Product Roadmap": "Instead of focusing on
  features to be developed, we focus on problems to be solved."; "We
  assign a KPI to each team which signifies if the problem has been
  solved successfully or not."
- Bastow, Now-Next-Later: "an outcome-focused product roadmap that
  organizes work by levels of confidence instead of fixed dates";
  "Link each Initiative to the OKRs it supports".
- McCarthy et al. (secondhand, talk notes): the roadmap is "A statement
  of intent and direction, not a promise of deliverables"; themes are
  "The problems / jobs to be done / needs of customers".
- Reforge/Mehta: the roadmap is "the sequence of features that
  implement the Product Strategy"; "Goals are at the bottom of the
  stack, not at the top, because goals should come from the roadmap".
  First Round: "It's important to document those concrete choices —
  not just that we've chosen to do A, but also to explicitly reinforce
  that we're *not* going to do B."

### F4 — Where it is now *(medium)*

- Perri: "It should be measured and quantified before the work
  starts."; the kata's "Sellers call office less than twice a week"
  against "We're not sure how often sellers are calling now".
- Bastow: "Now is the work in motion. These are validated Initiatives
  the team is actively working on, where the problem is well
  understood."
- Linear: "Initiative Health shows whether the latest initiative update
  indicated work was on track, at risk, or off track."
- GitHub changelog: release types "Release", "Improvement", "Retired";
  maturity "generally available" / "public preview".
- Wardley, "On being lost": map elements are "Visual representation,
  context specific, position of components relative to some form of
  anchor and movement of those components"; "Every single diagram I
  was using to determine strategy in business lacked one or more of
  those basic elements."

### F5 — How it has changed *(high that the forms exist and differ; medium on their separation)*

- keepachangelog 1.1.0: "A changelog is a file which contains a
  curated, chronologically ordered list of notable changes for each
  version of a project."; "Changelogs are for humans, not machines.";
  "Added… Changed… Deprecated… Removed… Fixed… Security"; "Using commit
  log diffs as changelogs is a bad idea: they're full of noise."; "Keep
  an Unreleased section at the top to track upcoming changes."
- Stripe changelog: named release lines with dated versions, a
  "Breaking change?" column, product grouping.
- GitLab: "For each release, the product manager is responsible for
  creating the MR and files for the feature release note."
- Linear Method: "Writing a changelog benefits both internal and
  external communication. Internally, it helps your team to track
  progress and reflect on what they have achieved."
- Charak, Product Decision Records: "Every decision has a context…";
  fields "Name, Date, Status (Open/Accepted/Rejected), Scope, Context,
  Decision, Consequences, Review Trigger"; "important for decisions to
  be revisited every so often."
- Productboard: "Organizational product memory is the shared record of
  what a product organization has learned. It captures your decisions,
  the reasons behind them, customer evidence, and competitive
  context". Metabase: "Institutional memory is a company's collective
  knowledge of what things mean, how they've changed, and who changed
  them."; "If something is in your face every day, you're more likely
  to keep it up to date."
- Quackback (vendor): the changelog creates "an institutional record of
  product decisions" — the one source conflating the two.

### F6 — Cross-context features *(high)*

- Evans, DDD Reference, Partnership: "Where development failure in
  either of two contexts would result in delivery failure for both,
  forge a partnership between the teams in charge of the two contexts.
  Institute a process for coordinated planning of development and

  cross-team collaboration."; "Autonomy requires alignment."

## Alternatives considered

- **Keep the brief as the first artifact and let the architect split
  cross-context requests ad hoc.** This is Spotify's documented gap; no
  opened source supports a per-team document as the first product
  artifact. Rejected.
- **Adopt LeSS: one product backlog, no context ownership.** It answers
  "requests against a product" directly but discards the
  context-owning shops the architecture principles and isolation rest
  on. Rejected as a whole; its single-backlog idea survives as the
  roadmap-of-initiatives.
- **Adopt Shape Up whole (pitches, betting, no backlog).** Its pitch is
  the best-formed product-level artifact found, and the appetite and
  no-gos are adopted into the initiative; its rejection of any backlog
  conflicts with the PO role's exclusive domain. Partial adoption.
- **Make the changelog the decision history (Quackback's claim).** The
  decision-record sources separate shipped from decided; conflating
  them loses the reasons. Rejected; both kept, linked.
- **Hand-drawn roadmap.** Every roadmap source warns it drifts into a
  feature list; generating it from initiative statuses keeps it true
  by construction (`single-source-of-truth`). Adopted.

## Limitations

- No controlled comparison of product processes exists; the evidence
  is practitioner texts and company practice, hence medium labels on
  consensus claims.
- Perri's strategy-deployment layers are secondhand; the Product
  Roadmaps Relaunched content is from talk notes.
- GitLab's handbook decision practices could not be read.
- The proposal's artifact names (initiative, product strategy) are the
  sources' most common; the authority may prefer the shop's own.
- What would change the judgment: a source showing that a persistent
  product-level artifact slows small teams more than ad hoc splitting
  costs them; or an authority decision that the framing itself should
  persist and carry the initiative's fields.

202	## H. Reforge / Ravi Mehta — Product Strategy Stack
203	
204	### H1. The Product Strategy Stack (Reforge blog)
205	URL: https://www.reforge.com/blog/the-product-strategy-stack (via r.jina.ai; direct fetch 403) — opened in full.
206	- Company mission: "The world your company sees and the change it wants to bring to that world."
207	- Company strategy: "The logical plan you have to bring your company's mission into being."
208	- Product strategy: "The logical plan for how the product will drive its part of the company strategy."
209	- Product roadmap: "How you sequence product strategy over time." / "the sequence of features that implement the Product Strategy."
210	- Product goals: "The outcomes that measure strategic progress."
211	- "The Product Roadmap should come before the Product Goals" because "a well-defined Product Roadmap helps teams focus on the important task of long-term value creation."
212	- "each layer is a prerequisite for the successive layer"; the stack is "the connective tissue between the objectives of the company and the product delivery work of the product team."
213	
214	### H2. First Round Review — Set "Non-Goals" and Build a Product Strategy Stack (Mehta interview)
215	URL: https://review.firstround.com/set-non-goals-and-build-a-product-strategy-stack-lessons-for-product-leaders/ — opened in full.
216	- "Product strategy is the connective tissue between what a product team is doing day-to-day and the company's ambition."
217	- "Goals are at the bottom of the stack, not at the top, because goals should come from the roadmap, not the other way around."
218	- "It's important to document those concrete choices — not just that we've chosen to do A, but also to explicitly reinforce that we're *not* going to do B."
219	- "As product leaders, every choice we make is a choice that we save our users from making. If we're not clear about what we want our product to do, we shift that lack of clarity to the user."
220	- "List out your next 100 days with the initial sequence for how you're going to start to build towards the north star for what the product looks like."
221	- "That's not a strategy, that's a goal. It's great if you can achieve that goal, but only if it's actually part of a larger strategy that the company is trying to advance."
222	Conflict: Reforge/Mehta define the roadmap as a "sequence of features" and put goals beneath the roadmap; Cagan (A4) and Perri (C1) put outcomes/problems first and treat feature roadmaps as the thing to convert. Both agree the artifact chain is mission → strategy → something sequenced → measures.
223	
224	## I. Linear — Linear Method and docs
225	
226	### I1. Linear Method — Introduction / Set the product direction
227	URLs: https://linear.app/method/introduction and https://linear.app/method/product-direction — opened in full.
228	- "Ambitious goals are the only way to make a significant impact. Companies should focus on them when they define their high-level direction."
229	- "All projects and work should directly correlate to these goals. Review projects and their target dates during initiative meetings and pull from projects as you plan cycles."
230	- "Initiatives are a critical tool for shaping this direction."
231	- "The process of creating initiatives and mapping out a product journey forces you to articulate a vision and decide how to build toward it."
232	- "Anyone in your company can look at the product initiatives to quickly understand what the most important streams of work are."
233	- "Writing a changelog benefits both internal and external communication. Internally, it helps your team to track progress and reflect on what they have achieved."
234	- "The clearest way to see whether something is complete or not is to show the diff in the code or design file."
235	
236	### I2. Linear Method — Write issues not user stories
237	URL: https://linear.app/method/write-issues-not-user-stories — opened in full.
238	- "User stories have become a cargo cult ritual that feels good but wastes a lot of resources and time."
239	- "They're a roundabout way to describe tasks, obscuring the work to be done."
240	- "Discuss the customer experience at the product level when you spec out projects and build your roadmap."
241	- "They'll understand the user experience intuitively, so you don't need to clarify it at the task level."
242	- "An issue should describe a task with a clear, defined outcome. This could be a piece of code, design, document, or action to be taken."
243	Note: Linear puts the user/problem context at project level (spec) and keeps issues as tasks — the problem artifact is the project, above the task.
244	
245	### I3. Linear docs — Initiatives; Projects
246	URLs: https://linear.app/docs/initiatives and https://linear.app/docs/projects — opened in full. (linear.app/method/projects → 404.)
247	- Initiatives: "Their purpose is to express the goals and objectives an organization aims to achieve and to monitor progress towards those aims." / "Use initiatives when you want an intentional set of projects tied to a shared objective." / "Designate a lead team to assign ownership over an initiative to a specific team."
248	- Projects: "Projects are units of work that have a clear outcome or planned completion date, such as a new feature's launch, and are comprised of issues and optional documents." / "They can be shared across multiple teams and come with their own unique features, progress graph, and notification options." / "Projects can be shared across multiple teams."
249	- Project overview holds "a brief project summary, project properties, any associated documents and links, a detailed project description, and a list of project milestones."
250	Note: Linear's model is initiative (objective, may have a lead team) → project (a feature-sized unit that can span several teams; carries spec + milestones + updates) → issue (task, owned by one team). This is the one source here that explicitly makes the feature-level artifact multi-team.
251	
252	## Cross-source observations (my reading, not quotes)
253	1. Every opened source places a written, product-level, problem-first artifact ahead of any feature or team assignment: opportunity assessment (A2), opportunity on the OST (B1), target condition/obstacle (C1–C2), pitch (D3), PR/FAQ (E1–E2), Intermission (F2), PRD problem section (G2), initiative (I1, I3). 255	3. Decision point is explicit and recorded in most: go/no-go (A2, E1), betting table (D4), initiative review (I1). Shape Up alone rejects a persistent backlog (D4).
256	4. The artifact often persists as the reference during build (E2 "touchstone", G2 open-issues/decision section, I3 project updates and milestones) — relevant to SQ2's "where is it / where next" question.
257	5. Multi-team features: only Linear (I3) states the feature-level unit "can be shared across multiple teams"; Intercom's hierarchy (F2) is per team objective; SVPG assigns problems "to the relevant product teams" (A4) without stating how a problem spanning teams is split. Gap to carry into SQ3.
