# SQ1 notes — the product-level problem/opportunity artifact at modern companies

Gathered 2026-08-26 via WebFetch/WebSearch. Status per source: opened in full (fetched, quotes extracted by the fetch tool from page content) / partial / could not be opened. Quotes are verbatim as returned by the fetch tool. Nothing below is summarized from memory; where a line is my reading rather than the source's words it is prefixed "Note:".

## A. SVPG / Marty Cagan

### A1. Product Strategy – Overview
URL: https://www.svpg.com/product-strategy-overview/ — opened in full.
- "how do we make the product vision a reality, while meeting the needs of the company as we go?"
- "product strategy helps us decide what problems to solve; product discovery helps us figure out the tactics that can actually solve the problems."
- "Choices means focus. Deciding what few things you really need to do, and therefore all the things you won't do."
- "insights come from analyzing the data and from learning from our customers. The insights might pertain to the dynamics of our business, our capabilities, new enabling technologies, the competitive landscape."
- "They have product teams that are more accurately feature teams, and they're slaving away, pounding out features all day, but rarely getting closer to their desired outcomes."
- "providing those teams with the strategic context necessary for them to solve the problems we need them to solve."
- "It requires four things that are not easy for most companies: choices on what's important; insights; converting insights into action; and active management."

### A2. Assessing Product Opportunities (the opportunity assessment)
URL: https://www.svpg.com/assessing-product-opportunities/ — opened in full.
- "The purpose of a good product opportunity assessment is either to a) prevent the company from wasting time and money on poor opportunities; or b) for those that are good opportunities, to understand what will be required to succeed."
- "I ask product managers to answer ten fundamental questions: 1. Exactly what problem will this solve? 2. For whom do we solve that problem? 3. How big is the opportunity?"
- "The hardest question to answer is usually the first, which surprises people because it sounds like the easiest."
- "Ask most product managers what problem their product is intended to solve, and you usually get a rambling list of features and capabilities, rather than the a crisp, clear and compelling statement of exactly the problem that's solved."
- "The purpose of the MRD is to describe the opportunity, not the solution...many companies don't really do MRD's, or if they do, they're essentially product specs that are called MRD's."
- "It is important that the results of the product opportunity assessment be presented and discussed with senior management, and that the company make a clear go or no-go decision."
Note: this is the closest SVPG analogue to a product-level problem statement: a short document per opportunity, problem-first, ending in a go/no-go decision, explicitly distinct from a spec.

### A3. Product vs Feature Teams
URL: https://www.svpg.com/product-vs-feature-teams/ — opened in full.
- Feature teams: "they are there to _serve the business_" and are given "a prioritized list that is called the roadmap".
- Product teams: "they are _empowered_ to figure out the best way to solve the problems they've been asked to solve".
- "the product manager is explicitly responsible for ensuring _value_ and _viability_" (product teams) vs. "the _value and business viability are the responsibility of the stakeholder or executive that requested the feature_" (feature teams).
- "the _purpose_ of a product team in this sense _is to solve problems in ways our customers love, yet work for our business_".
- "These feature teams will often think they are doing product discovery, but really it's just design and maybe a little usability testing".

### A4. Changing How You Decide Which Problems To Solve (Jon Moore & Marty Cagan)
URL: https://www.svpg.com/changing-how-you-decide-which-problems-to-solve/ — opened in full.
- "This is not a difficult step, but simply providing your empowered product teams with problems to solve, and clear measures of success, can go a long way towards generating better solutions."
- "It is not hard to simply take your existing product roadmaps, and for each feature or project, to determine what the underlying problem to solve is."
- "A strong product vision will inspire an organization for many years (most are 3-10 year product visions)."
- "The product strategy begins by focusing on the most critical areas for business success."
- "The product strategy identifies the most critical problems to solve in the quarter, and the product leaders assign those problems to the relevant product teams."
- "We are constantly investigating the quantitative insights, mainly derived from the data that's generated; and also the qualitative insights."
Note: the chain here is vision (years) → strategy (focus + insights) → quarterly problems to solve → assigned to teams; the problem, not the feature, is the unit handed to a team.

### A5. Product Vision vs. Mission
URL: https://www.svpg.com/product-vision-vs-mission/ — opened in full.
- "A good product vision keeps us focused on the customer" and "serves as the North Star for the product organization so that we have a common understanding of what we are hoping to accomplish together."
- "When each team has their own vision, it's the equivalent of everyone picking out their own star from the sky, and calling it their 'north star' and then heading in their own direction."
- "The product vision, combined with the annual company objectives, drives the product strategy."
- The vision "provides the engineering organization with enough clarity about what's coming in the next several years so they can ensure they have in place an architecture that can serve the need."

### A6. "Problems to solve, not features to build" — could not be opened
URL tried: https://www.svpg.com/problems-to-solve-not-features-to-build/ (direct and via r.jina.ai) — redirects to SVPG home; article body not retrieved. Not cited. A4 covers the same claim from a page that did open.

## B. Product Talk / Teresa Torres

### B1. Opportunity Solution Trees (main page)
URL: https://www.producttalk.org/opportunity-solution-trees/ — opened in full. (Also https://www.producttalk.org/opportunity-solution-tree/ opened, same content.)
- "Opportunity solution trees are a simple way of visually representing the paths you might take to reach a desired outcome."
- "The root of the tree is your desired outcome—the business need that reflects how your team can create business value."
- "The outcome at the top of an opportunity solution tree sets the scope for discovery. It helps teams understand which opportunities are relevant and keeps them focused on the right types of solutions."
- "An opportunity is an unmet customer need, pain point, or desire."
- "A solution is a product, a service, or a feature that we offer to address an opportunity. The opportunity represents the underlying need, pain point, or desire."
- "The best way to test if an opportunity is really a solution in disguise is to ask, 'Is there more than one way to address this opportunity?'"
- "Below the solution space are assumption tests. This is how we'll evaluate which solutions will help us best create customer value."
- "One of the key benefits of using an opportunity solution tree is it helps your team externalize and visualize your thinking, so it's easier to align around what to do when."
- "An opportunity solution tree is a living document that should evolve as you learn from your discovery activities."
Note: the opportunity is a product-level artifact that lives independent of any solution/feature; features hang beneath it, and several features may address one opportunity. The tree is per team (rooted in the team's outcome), not per component.

### B2. "The difference between opportunities and solutions" — could not be opened
URL tried: https://www.producttalk.org/2021/05/opportunities-vs-solutions/ — 404. Search found no standalone post with that title; the distinction is carried in B1 ("solution in disguise"). Not cited separately.

## C. Melissa Perri

### C1. What is Good Product Strategy?
URL: https://melissaperri.com/blog/2016/07/14/what-is-good-product-strategy (via r.jina.ai) — opened in full.
- "This isn't a strategy, this is a plan. The problem is that when we treat a product strategy like a plan, it will almost always fail."
- "Product Strategy is a system of achievable goals and visions that work together to align the team around desirable outcomes for both the business and your customers."
- "The vision is your high level, ultimate view of where the company or business line is going...Think long term here, and keep it qualitative."
- "The challenge is the first Business goal you have to achieve on the way to your longer term vision...a strategic objective that helps align and focus your team."
- "The target condition helps break down the Challenge. Challenges are made up of smaller problems you need to tackle along the way...achievable, measurable metrics."
- "This is what the current reality is compared to the Target Condition. It should be measured and quantified before the work starts."
- "It's the Product Manager and their team's responsibility to determine the user problems and other obstacles standing in the way of achieving that Target Condition."

### C2. The Product Kata
URL: https://melissaperri.com/blog/2015/07/22/the-product-kata — opened in full (worked example).
- Vision: "Make our sellers completely self sufficient in managing their stores."
- Target condition: "Sellers call office less than twice a week".
- Obstacle: "We're not sure how often sellers are calling now".
- "We weren't building new features for the sellers...we wanted to learn quickly".
- "Every step you take, you also say how you will measure its progress. A step with no measurements can't tell you if you are improving."
Note: the kata records current condition → target condition → obstacle → experiment, so the artifact itself carries "where we are / where next" as a measured pair.

### C3. Strategy deployment (vision → strategic intents → product initiatives → options) — secondhand only
melissaperri.com/blog/2019/11/1/strategy-deployment → 404. Search results (smartproductpeople.substack.com, medium.com/@lindadao92) report the four-layer model from *Escaping the Build Trap*; not opened as primary. Marked secondhand; cite only as such.

## D. Basecamp — Shape Up

### D1. Principles of Shaping
URL: https://basecamp.com/shapeup/1.1-chapter-02 — opened in full.
- "Work in the shaping stage is rough. Everyone can tell by looking at it that it's unfinished."
- "Despite being rough and unfinished, shaped work has been thought through. All the main elements of the solution are there."
- "Shaped work indicates what not to do. It tells the team where to stop."
- "When design leaders go straight to wireframes or high-fidelity mockups, they define too much detail too early."
- "When a project is defined in a few words, nobody knows what it means."
- "We have two separate tracks: one for shaping, one for building. During any six week cycle, the teams are building work that's been previously shaped."
- "Setting the appetite and coming up with a solution requires you to be critical about the problem."

### D2. Set Boundaries
URL: https://basecamp.com/shapeup/1.2-chapter-03 — opened in full.
- "You can think of the appetite as a time budget for a standard team size."
- "Appetites start with a number and end with a design. We use the appetite as a creative constraint on the design process."
- "Our default response to any idea that comes up should be: 'Interesting. Maybe some day.' In other words, a very soft 'no' that leaves all our options open."
- Reframing: from "What could we build?" to "What's really going wrong?"
- "When someone proposes something like 'redesign the Files section,' that's a grab-bag, not a project."
- "The insight wasn't 'computerize the calendar'—that's obvious. What we learned was that 'see free spaces' was the important thing."
- "The best is relative to your constraints. Without a time limit, there's always a better version."

### D3. Write the Pitch
URL: https://basecamp.com/shapeup/1.5-chapter-06 — opened in full.
- Five ingredients: "Problem — The raw idea, a use case, or something we've seen that motivates us to work on this"; "Appetite — How much time we want to spend and how that constrains the solution"; "Solution — The core elements we came up with, presented in a form that's easy for people to immediately understand"; "Rabbit holes — Details about the solution worth calling out to avoid problems"; "No-gos — Anything specifically excluded from the concept: functionality or use cases we intentionally aren't covering".
- "The purpose of the pitch is to present a good potential bet. It's basically a presentation."
- "People comment on the pitch asynchronously. Not to say yes or no — that happens at the betting table — but to poke holes or contribute missing information."

### D4. Bets, Not Backlogs
URL: https://basecamp.com/shapeup/2.1-chapter-07 — opened in full.
- "Backlogs are a big weight we don't need to carry. Dozens and eventually hundreds of tasks pile up that we all know we'll never have time for."
- "Before each six-week cycle, we hold a betting table where stakeholders decide what to do in the next cycle."
- "There's no giant list of ideas to review. There's no time spent grooming a backlog of old ideas. There are just a few well-shaped, risk-reduced options to review."
- "If we decide to bet on a pitch, it goes into the next cycle to build. If we don't, we let it go. There's nothing we need to track or hold on to."
- "Anything brought back is brought back with a context, by a person, with a purpose. Everything is relevant, timely, and of the moment."
Note: Shape Up's unit is the pitch — problem + appetite + rough solution + boundaries — at product level, bet on by stakeholders; the team, not the pitch, is scoped after the bet. Conflict with A/B: Shape Up hands teams a shaped solution, not only a problem; Cagan/Torres hand teams a problem/outcome and leave the solution to the team.

## E. Amazon — Working Backwards / PR-FAQ

### E1. workingbackwards.com — PR/FAQ process (Bryar & Carr)
URL: https://workingbackwards.com/concepts/working-backwards-pr-faq-process/ — opened in full. (Homepage https://www.workingbackwards.com/ opened; /the-pr-faq 404.)
- "Working Backwards is a systematic way to vet ideas and create new products. Its key tenet is to start by defining the customer experience, then iteratively work backwards from that point until the team achieves clarity of thought around what to build."
- "Writing a press release is a forcing function to ensure that the creator of the new product idea is focused on the customer."
- "Problem Paragraph: This is where you describe the problem(s) that your product is designed to solve. Make sure you write this paragraph from the customer's point of view."
- "A well-written PR defines a specific objective– a destination where there is a treasure. Think of the FAQ section as the map to that destination and a detailed description of the dragons you will need to slay along your journey."
- "A well-written internal FAQ section anticipates the most important questions that senior leaders and stakeholders in the company will ask after reading the PR."
- "The best PR/FAQs are produced through an iterative process requiring discussion, debate, and collaboration with many stakeholders."
- "If the new idea is a go, what happens next should be well understood because it is described in the FAQs. In other words, resources (people, money, fixed cost investments), a rough timeline, and other operational matters are spelled out in the document."
- "Once the PR/FAQ is finalized and approved, the Agile process can be employed to build the product. Amazon frequently used Agile in conjunction with the PR/FAQ process."

### E2. Ian McAllister, Quora answer (2012) on Amazon's approach
URL: https://www.quora.com/What-is-Amazons-approach-to-product-development-and-product-management (via r.jina.ai) — opened in full.
- "We try to work backwards from the customer, rather than starting with an idea for a product and trying to bolt customers onto it."
- "If the benefits listed don't sound very interesting or exciting to customers, then perhaps they're not (and shouldn't be built)."
- "Iterating on a press release is a lot less expensive than iterating on the product itself (and quicker!)."
- "Keep it simple. 3-4 sentences for most paragraphs. Cut out the fat."
- "Once the project moves into development, the press release can be used as a touchstone; a guiding light." / "The product team can ask themselves, 'Are we building what is in the press release?'"
- "This keeps product development focused on achieving the customer benefits and not building extraneous stuff."
(McAllister's Medium repost: 404, not opened.)
Note: the PR/FAQ is product-level, precedes any team decomposition, is decided go/no-go, and remains the reference during build — i.e. it doubles as the "where we are going" record for that initiative.

## F. Intercom

### F1. RICE prioritization
URL: https://www.intercom.com/blog/rice-simple-prioritization-for-product-managers/ — opened in full.
- "Estimate how many people each project will affect within a given period." (Reach)
- "Factor in your level of confidence about your estimates. If you think a project could have huge impact but don't have data to back it up, confidence lets you control that."
- "Estimate the total amount of time a project will require from all members of your team: product, design, and engineering." (Effort)
- "A good prioritization framework can help you consider each factor about a project idea with clear-eyed discipline and combine those factors in a rigorous, consistent way."
- "RICE scores shouldn't be used as a hard and fast rule. There are many reasons why you might work on a project with a lower score first."

### F2. Lessons learned from scaling a product team (the "Intermission" brief)
URL: https://www.intercom.com/blog/how-we-build-software/ — opened in full (title: "Lessons learned from scaling a product team").
- "The Intermission is our quirky name for a project brief...It never includes solutions because this comes later."
- "This document is the responsibility of the Product Manager...restricted to less than one page and must succinctly cover the problem we're solving."
- "Everything in our roadmap is broken down by team objective, which is broken down into multiple projects, which in turn are broken down into individual releases."
- "All our projects are scoped into small independent releases that add value to customers...reduce scope and simplify, in order to move faster."
- "The outcome matters much more than the plan...Plans are made with the information available at the time but only become fully clear as you execute them."
Note: Intercom's one-page problem-only brief sits between roadmap objective and project; hierarchy objective → project → release.

## G. Lenny's Newsletter / startup PRD templates

### G1. My favorite PM templates (issue 37)
URL: https://www.lennysnewsletter.com/p/my-favorite-templates-issue-37 (via r.jina.ai) — opened in full (index page; templates are external Google/Coda docs).
- On Square (Kevin Yien) PRD: "Love this whole template, particularly the "Non-Goals" section and the step-by-step flow".
- On Asana project brief: "Also love this whole template, particularly the problem statement framework".
- On Intercom story template: "Love the simplicity, while still having everything you need to get started".
- On Adam Waxman (SeatGeek) PRD: "Love 1-pager summary section before it dives deep".
- On Steve Morin (Asana) 1-pager: "Love the focus on success criteria and risks".
- "A reminder of how valuable it is to keep these to one page, at least to start".
Template URLs recorded: Square https://docs.google.com/document/d/1mEMDcHmtQ6twzNlpvF-9maNlAcezpWDtCnyIqWkODZs/edit ; Asana brief https://docs.google.com/document/d/1W46cmPfPwXIIH2mNNbbQ5EdjnhQFqGxGhT5iAijmJjc/edit ; Product Hunt https://docs.google.com/document/d/1yrU5F6Gxhkfma91wf_IbZfexw8_fahbGQLW3EvwdfQI/edit ; SeatGeek https://docs.google.com/document/d/1xc9TZX-7NMfOykzFKR0o0jzTUygoAFzWadxDVR7sNvs/edit ; Asana 1-pager https://docs.google.com/document/d/1BeNK9BYd3-8pAqVYR_B0Gzp7kGNtWdPFHJKIXI52_84/edit — none of the Google Docs opened.

### G2. Figma's approach to PRDs (Yuhki Yamashita, Coda)
URL: https://coda.io/@yuhki/figmas-approach-to-product-requirement-docs/prd-name-of-project-1 — opened in full.
- Problem: "Describe the problem (or opportunity) you're trying to solve. Why is it important to our users and our business?"
- High-level approach: "Describe briefly the approach you're taking to solve this problem. This should be enough for the reader to imagine possible solution directions."
- Goals & success: "What does success look like? What metrics are you intending to move? Explain why these metrics are important if not obvious."
- Key features: "Give an overview of what we're building. Provide an organized list of features, with priorities if relevant."
- Open issues: "Keep track of open issues / key decisions here. Sometimes, certain decisions are made that might feel controversial; document these here."
- Timeline: "Identify any relevant milestones (e.g., a Dogfood or Beta milestone) that people should know about."
Note: at Figma the PRD is one document per project that carries problem, approach, features, and a running decision log together — the feature list is a section inside the problem document, not a separate artifact.

### G3. "How to write a good PRD" — could not be opened
URL: https://www.lennysnewsletter.com/p/how-to-write-a-good-prd (direct and via r.jina.ai) — body absent/paywalled. Not cited.

## H. Reforge / Ravi Mehta — Product Strategy Stack

### H1. The Product Strategy Stack (Reforge blog)
URL: https://www.reforge.com/blog/the-product-strategy-stack (via r.jina.ai; direct fetch 403) — opened in full.
- Company mission: "The world your company sees and the change it wants to bring to that world."
- Company strategy: "The logical plan you have to bring your company's mission into being."
- Product strategy: "The logical plan for how the product will drive its part of the company strategy."
- Product roadmap: "How you sequence product strategy over time." / "the sequence of features that implement the Product Strategy."
- Product goals: "The outcomes that measure strategic progress."
- "The Product Roadmap should come before the Product Goals" because "a well-defined Product Roadmap helps teams focus on the important task of long-term value creation."
- "each layer is a prerequisite for the successive layer"; the stack is "the connective tissue between the objectives of the company and the product delivery work of the product team."

### H2. First Round Review — Set "Non-Goals" and Build a Product Strategy Stack (Mehta interview)
URL: https://review.firstround.com/set-non-goals-and-build-a-product-strategy-stack-lessons-for-product-leaders/ — opened in full.
- "Product strategy is the connective tissue between what a product team is doing day-to-day and the company's ambition."
- "Goals are at the bottom of the stack, not at the top, because goals should come from the roadmap, not the other way around."

## I. Linear — Linear Method and docs

### I1. Linear Method — Introduction / Set the product direction
URLs: https://linear.app/method/introduction and https://linear.app/method/product-direction — opened in full.
- "Ambitious goals are the only way to make a significant impact. Companies should focus on them when they define their high-level direction."
- "All projects and work should directly correlate to these goals. Review projects and their target dates during initiative meetings and pull from projects as you plan cycles."
- "Initiatives are a critical tool for shaping this direction."
- "The process of creating initiatives and mapping out a product journey forces you to articulate a vision and decide how to build toward it."
- "Anyone in your company can look at the product initiatives to quickly understand what the most important streams of work are."
- "Writing a changelog benefits both internal and external communication. Internally, it helps your team to track progress and reflect on what they have achieved."
- "The clearest way to see whether something is complete or not is to show the diff in the code or design file."

### I2. Linear Method — Write issues not user stories
URL: https://linear.app/method/write-issues-not-user-stories — opened in full.
- "User stories have become a cargo cult ritual that feels good but wastes a lot of resources and time."
- "They're a roundabout way to describe tasks, obscuring the work to be done."
- "Discuss the customer experience at the product level when you spec out projects and build your roadmap."
- "They'll understand the user experience intuitively, so you don't need to clarify it at the task level."
- "An issue should describe a task with a clear, defined outcome. This could be a piece of code, design, document, or action to be taken."
Note: Linear puts the user/problem context at project level (spec) and keeps issues as tasks — the problem artifact is the project, above the task.

### I3. Linear docs — Initiatives; Projects
URLs: https://linear.app/docs/initiatives and https://linear.app/docs/projects — opened in full. (linear.app/method/projects → 404.)
- Initiatives: "Their purpose is to express the goals and objectives an organization aims to achieve and to monitor progress towards those aims." / "Use initiatives when you want an intentional set of projects tied to a shared objective." / "Designate a lead team to assign ownership over an initiative to a specific team."
- Projects: "Projects are units of work that have a clear outcome or planned completion date, such as a new feature's launch, and are comprised of issues and optional documents." / "They can be shared across multiple teams and come with their own unique features, progress graph, and notification options." / "Projects can be shared across multiple teams."
- Project overview holds "a brief project summary, project properties, any associated documents and links, a detailed project description, and a list of project milestones."
Note: Linear's model is initiative (objective, may have a lead team) → project (a feature-sized unit that can span several teams; carries spec + milestones + updates) → issue (task, owned by one team). This is the one source here that explicitly makes the feature-level artifact multi-team.

## Cross-source observations (my reading, not quotes)
1. Every opened source places a written, product-level, problem-first artifact ahead of any feature or team assignment: opportunity assessment (A2), opportunity on the OST (B1), target condition/obstacle (C1–C2), pitch (D3), PR/FAQ (E1–E2), Intermission (F2), PRD problem section (G2), initiative (I1, I3). 2. Two schools on what the team receives: problem/outcome only (Cagan A3–A4, Torres B1, Perri C1) vs. a shaped solution with boundaries (Shape Up D1–D3) or an approved PR/FAQ (E1). Recorded as a conflict; both agree the decision is taken at product level before the team starts.
3. Decision point is explicit and recorded in most: go/no-go (A2, E1), betting table (D4), initiative review (I1). Shape Up alone rejects a persistent backlog (D4).
4. The artifact often persists as the reference during build (E2 "touchstone", G2 open-issues/decision section, I3 project updates and milestones) — relevant to SQ2's "where is it / where next" question.
5. Multi-team features: only Linear (I3) states the feature-level unit "can be shared across multiple teams"; Intercom's hierarchy (F2) is per team objective; SVPG assigns problems "to the relevant product teams" (A4) without stating how a problem spanning teams is split. Gap to carry into SQ3.

# SQ2 notes — where the product has been / is / is going, as artifacts (modern startups and tech companies)

Gathered 2026-08-26. Status legend: OPENED = read in full via fetch; ABSTRACT = only a summary/extract reachable; UNOPENED = could not be opened. All quotes verbatim from the opened page. Fetches go through a summarising reader, so passages are as returned by it; nothing is from memory.

## A. Roadmaps as "where we are going" (and, in Now/Next/Later, "where we are")

### 1. Janna Bastow (ProdPad), "Now-Next-Later roadmap" — OPENED
URL: https://www.prodpad.com/blog/now-next-later-roadmap/  (by Janna Bastow; page states "Updated: June 29th, 2026"; reviewed by Simon Cast)
- "A Now-Next-Later roadmap is an outcome-focused product roadmap that organizes work by levels of confidence instead of fixed dates."
- "The timeline roadmap is the format Now-Next-Later was built to replace, swapping dated columns for confidence horizons."
- "Link each Initiative to the OKRs it supports, so the commitment lives on the objective."
- "Now is the work in motion. These are validated Initiatives the team is actively working on, where the problem is well understood."
- "A Now-Next-Later roadmap is not a queue of work moving toward delivery. It is a system for reducing uncertainty through discovery."
Relevance: the roadmap's unit is an *initiative* (a problem/outcome), not a feature; the "Now" column is the artifact that says "where we are"; the tie to OKRs is how "why" is carried. Note the page does not itself describe a "Completed/Done" column — the "where we've been" answer is not claimed by this page.

### 2. Marty Cagan (SVPG), "The Alternative to Roadmaps" — OPENED
URL: https://www.svpg.com/the-alternative-to-roadmaps/  (Marty Cagan, September 7, 2015)
- "Unfortunately, typical roadmaps do just what the General warned against – they tell the team what to do."
- "In several articles I have highlighted the reasons I see typical product roadmaps as the source of so much waste in product teams."
- "The Product Vision: this describes the holistic view of what the organization as a whole is trying to accomplish. The Business Objectives: this describes the specific, prioritized business objectives for each product team."
- "Tell the team what you need them to accomplish, and how the results will be measured, and let the team figure out the best way to solve the problems."
- "The team is not off the hook just by delivering a requested feature or project; the feature must actually work (as measured by the key results) otherwise the team needs to try a different approach."
- "It is all about outcome rather than output."
- "We address this with the concept of high-integrity commitments. We do this for those situations where we need to actually commit to a date or a specific deliverable."
Relevance: "where we are going" = product vision + prioritised business objectives per team; the feature roadmap is explicitly rejected as the direction artifact; dated commitments are the exception ("high-integrity commitments"), not the roadmap.

### 3. Marty Cagan (SVPG), "Team Objectives – Overview" — OPENED
URL: https://www.svpg.com/team-objectives-overview/  (Marty Cagan, February 24, 2020)
- "The OKR technique came from companies that had empowered product teams in their DNA. OKR's are first and foremost an empowerment technique."
- "The main idea is to give product teams real problems to solve, and then to give the teams the space to solve them."
- Companies "think they can 'check the empowerment box' by giving the team objectives, yet still continue to tell them the solutions they are supposed to deliver – nearly always in the form of a roadmap of features."
- "Leaders need to step up and do their part to turn product strategy into action" (reader's paraphrase-quote of the page; treat as near-verbatim).
Relevance: OKRs are the "where next" artifact at team level, and they are supposed to be *problems*, derived from product strategy, not features.

### 4. Melissa Perri, "Rethinking the Product Roadmap" — OPENED
URL: https://melissaperri.com/blog/2014/05/19/rethinking-the-product-roadmap  (Melissa Perri, May 19, 2014)
- "Instead of focusing on features to be developed, we focus on problems to be solved."
- "It's broken into two phases: Discover & Experiment and Build & Validate."
- "Each cross-functional team works on a problem to be solved during the time frame. Their goal is to the solve the problem. We assign a KPI to each team which signifies if the problem has been solved successfully or not."
- "The roadmap is flexible since problems are constantly being evaluated, and irrelevant problems will be squashed at the beginning of each cycle."
- "We can communicate the problems we plan on tackling to the team and our customers without committing to solutions we do not know will solve the problem."
Relevance: the "problem roadmap" — the roadmap row is a problem with a KPI and a team; this is the closest published form to a "product-level problem statement with a home" that also tells direction. Reader noted the post does not tie to vision explicitly.

### 5. Melissa Perri, "What is Good Product Strategy?" — OPENED
URL: https://melissaperri.com/blog/2016/07/14/what-is-good-product-strategy  (Melissa Perri, July 14, 2016)
- "Product Strategy is a system of achievable goals and visions that work together to align the team around desirable outcomes for both the business and your customers."
- "The vision is your high level, ultimate view of where the company or business line is going."
- "The challenge is the first Business goal you have to achieve on the way to your longer term vision."
- "Target condition helps break down the Challenge...set in terms of achievable, measurable metrics."
- "This isn't a strategy, this is a plan. The problem is that when we treat a product strategy like a plan, it will almost always fail."
Relevance: Perri's strategy stack (Vision → Challenge → Target condition → current state, worked by the Product Kata) has an explicit *current state* element — a measured "where we are" — which few of the other artifacts make explicit. Secondary accounts (search only, not opened) name the later book-era terms "Vision, Strategic Intent, Product Initiatives, and Options" — knowledge-only / secondhand.

### 6. Lombardo, McCarthy, Ryan, Connors, "Product Roadmaps Relaunched" (O'Reilly 2017) — book UNOPENED; secondary notes OPENED
Book URL (unopened): https://www.oreilly.com/library/view/product-roadmaps-relaunched/9781491971710/
Secondary (opened, via r.jina.ai): https://walkerux.wordpress.com/2018/07/09/notes-on-bruce-mccarthys-roadmaps-relaunched/  — reader's notes from a 2018 talk; treat as secondhand.
- Roadmap is "A strategic communication tool" and "A statement of intent and direction, not a promise of deliverables."
- Vision: "How a specific customer will benefit from your product as it becomes more fully-realized and ubiquitous."
- Business Objectives: "What will be measurably different for the org as you progress towards your product vision."
- Timeframes: "Should be kept broad (quarterly for example) rather than having specific delivery dates."
- Themes: "The problems / jobs to be done / needs of customers that you plan to fulfill while you drive towards product vision and business objectives."
- "It's NOT a release plan" and should not "Act as a project plan or a release plan."
- "Disclaimers set the expectation that everything is subject to change — it's even likely to change as you iteratively learn."
Second secondary (search snippet only, not opened): https://awesomeproductsquad.medium.com/what-i-learned-from-bruce-mccarthys-product-roadmap-workshop-878a6557ecef — lists the same five primary components (vision, business outcomes, timeframes, themes) with Now/Next/Later or H1/H2 as timeframes.
Relevance: convergence with Bastow, Cagan, Perri — the roadmap's rows are *themes = problems*, direction not delivery.

## B. Linear — projects / initiatives / cycles / changelog as one linked record

### 7. Linear Method, "Introduction" (Principles & Practices) — OPENED
URL: https://linear.app/method/introduction
- Section "Set strategic product initiatives": "Ambitious goals are the only way to make a significant impact." "Companies should focus on them when they define their high-level direction."
- Section "Meaningful direction": "It's important to understand and remind everyone of the purpose and long-term goals of your work."
- Section "Work in n-week cycles": "Cycles create a healthy routine and focus teams on what needs to happen next." "2-week cycles are the most common in software building."
- Section "Scope issues to be as small as possible": "Break down work into smaller parts and create an issue for each one when possible."
- Section "Write a changelog": "Writing a changelog benefits both internal and external communication." "It keeps users informed about what's new and demonstrates commitment to improving the product."
- Section "Measure progress with actual work": "The clearest way to see whether something is complete or not is to show the diff in the code or design file."
(The sub-page https://linear.app/method/write-a-changelog returned 404 — UNOPENED.)

### 8. Linear Method, "Set the product direction" — OPENED
URL: https://linear.app/method/product-direction
- "A clear direction aligns everyone to work toward the same goals. It helps individuals make daily decisions, teams prioritize projects, and all members of your organization feel motivated toward a shared purpose."
- "Initiatives are a critical tool for shaping this direction. The process of creating initiatives and mapping out a product journey forces you to articulate a vision and decide how to build toward it."
- "The culminating product timeline sets a path of execution for the near future, slightly in front of you, and ideally a bit out of reach."
- "Anyone in your company can look at the product initiatives to quickly understand what the most important streams of work are, why they matter, and how they are progressing."
- "Visible initiatives motivate individuals by giving them context on why their work matters and create a culture of transparency that builds trust."

### 9. Linear docs, "Initiatives" and "Projects" — OPENED
URLs: https://linear.app/docs/initiatives ; https://linear.app/docs/projects
Initiatives:
- "Their purpose is to express the goals and objectives an organization aims to achieve and to monitor progress towards those aims."
- "Use initiatives when you want an intentional set of projects tied to a shared objective. Use project views when you want work to be collected automatically based on filters."
- "Initiative Health shows whether the latest initiative update indicated work was on track, at risk, or off track."
- "Communicate the current stage of the initiative using available statuses—Proposed, Planned, Active, Completed, or Canceled."
- "Leadership can use the top-level Initiatives view to see a quick overview of ongoing goals, objectives, and their progress."
Projects:
- "Projects are units of work that have a clear outcome or planned completion date, such as a new feature's launch, and are comprised of issues and optional documents."
- Project page holds "a brief project summary, project properties, any associated documents and links, a detailed project description, and a list of project milestones."
Relevance: Linear's hierarchy Initiative (objective, status lifecycle Proposed→Completed/Canceled, health from dated updates) → Project (outcome-bounded, spans teams, carries docs) → Issue (per team). A project is the artifact for a feature that crosses teams; the initiative is the product-level direction record; the completed/cancelled statuses plus dated updates give the "where we've been" trail.

### 10. Linear changelog — OPENED
URL: https://linear.app/changelog
- Reverse-chronological dated entries with a headline per release, e.g. "August 20, 2026: Coding sessions: environments, browser use, and updated pricing"; "August 13, 2026: Team initiatives"; "July 30, 2026: Coding sessions on mobile".
- Each entry: main heading, plain-language description (e.g. "Linear Agent can now set up, run, and test your code before returning its work"), sub-sections, and grouped "Fixes", "Improvements", "Keyboard shortcuts", "MCP server", "API" lists.
Relevance: a weekly, curated, product-language narrative of change — the public "how has the product changed" record.

## C. Changelogs and release notes as product history

### 11. keepachangelog.com v1.1.0 — OPENED
URL: https://keepachangelog.com/en/1.1.0/
- "A changelog is a file which contains a curated, chronologically ordered list of notable changes for each version of a project."
- Why: "To make it easier for users and contributors to see precisely what notable changes have been made between each release (or version) of the project."
- Guiding principles: "Changelogs are for humans, not machines. There should be an entry for every single version. The same types of changes should be grouped. Versions and sections should be linkable. The latest version comes first."
- Types: "Added for new features. Changed for changes in existing functionality. Deprecated for soon-to-be removed features. Removed for now removed features. Fixed for any bug fixes. Security in case of vulnerabilities."
- "Using commit log diffs as changelogs is a bad idea: they're full of noise."
- "Keep an Unreleased section at the top to track upcoming changes. People can see what changes they might expect in upcoming releases."
- "Yanked releases are versions that had to be pulled because of a serious bug or security issue."
Relevance: an established external form (principle external-standards-first) for the "what changed" record; the Unreleased section is a small "where next" inside the history artifact; curated, not generated from commits.

### 12. Stripe changelog — OPENED
URL: https://docs.stripe.com/changelog
- Organised by named release lines ("Dahlia", "Clover", "Basil") each holding dated versions such as "2026-07-29.dahlia" and a parallel "2026-07-29.preview".
- Each entry is a table row with a "Breaking change?" column marked "Breaking" or "Non-breaking", a "Category" column ("api" or "stripejs"), and product grouping ("Billing and invoicing", "Connect", "Payments", "Tax", "Terminal").
- Each row links to its own page, e.g. "Adds invoice description, footer, and custom parameters to the Subscription Schedules and Quotes APIs".
Relevance: history keyed to *versions of the contract* (API version), with breaking-ness and product area as first-class fields; preview versions publish "where next" for breaking changes before they land.

### 13. GitHub changelog — OPENED
URL: https://github.blog/changelog/
- Entries organised by month/year, each dated and tagged by product area; release types "Release", "Improvement", "Retired"; maturity markers "generally available" / "public preview".
- Sample entries: "Aug. 26: GitHub Apps can now access enterprise billing data"; "Aug. 7: Copilot code review effort levels are generally available".
Relevance: history record carries lifecycle state (preview → GA → retired) per change, so the changelog also says where each capability *is*.

### 14. GitLab release notes (docs) — OPENED (handbook release-post page redirected here)
URL: https://docs.gitlab.com/development/documentation/release_notes/  (redirect from https://handbook.gitlab.com/handbook/marketing/blog/release-posts/)
- "GitLab release notes are stored in the `gitlab` repository", one directory per release with an index and "individual files for each feature".
- "The following features are being delivered for GitLab <version>. These features are now available on GitLab.com."
- "For each release, the product manager is responsible for creating the MR and files for the feature release note. The Technical writing team is responsible for creating all other directories and files."
Relevance: release notes are PM-owned, versioned in the product repo, one file per feature — history as a governed artifact with a named owner.

### 15. Quackback, "Keep a Changelog: The Definitive Guide for Product Teams" — OPENED (vendor blog; practitioner-grade, undated in extract)
URL: https://quackback.io/blog/keep-a-changelog
- "Users learn what is new, what is fixed, and what they need to do differently. Your team tracks what shipped and when, creating an institutional record of product decisions. Support teams answer questions about recent changes without reading code diffs or pinging engineering."
- "Internal tools benefit from changelogs too — they reduce 'what changed?' questions from colleagues and create a record of decisions."
Relevance: the only opened piece stating outright that the changelog is the team's "institutional record of product decisions" — the "changelog as product memory" claim; single vendor source, medium-low weight.

## D. Decision records and product memory

### 16. Dinker Charak, "Product Decision Records" — OPENED
URL: https://www.dinker.in/product-decision-records/  (Dinker Charak, July 4, 2021)
- "Every decision has a context... it is important to note the context under which a decision regarding the product was taken."
- "It is an important tool to help teams that work on the products after you understand the decisions and make better calls as the product evolves."
- Fields: Name, Date, Status (Open/Accepted/Rejected), Scope, Context, Decision, Consequences, Review Trigger, optional Author(s).
- "All decisions are taken at a moment in time and have a context. Thus it is important for decisions to be revisited every so often."
Relevance: PDR = ADR form applied to product decisions, with an explicit *Review Trigger* field. Reader noted the post does not itself cite ADRs. Search also found generic "decision log" templates (LaunchNotes, Aha!, Plane) — UNOPENED, listed for completeness: https://www.launchnotes.com/glossary/decision-log-template-in-product-management-and-operations ; https://www.aha.io/roadmapping/guide/templates/create/decision-log ; https://plane.so/blog/decision-log-what-it-is-why-teams-use-it-and-template ; https://github.com/joelparkerhenderson/decision-record

### 17. Productboard, "What is organizational product memory?" — OPENED (vendor)
URL: https://www.productboard.com/blog/what-is-organizational-product-memory/  (Productboard, July 30, 2026)
- "Organizational product memory is the shared record of what a product organization has learned. It captures your decisions, the reasons behind them, customer evidence, and competitive context, and it lives in your team's tools rather than in individual people's heads."
- Four components named: "Decision rationale", "Customer evidence", "Competitive context", "Strategy and personas".
Relevance: recent vendor framing of "where we've been" as decisions-plus-rationale, not shipped features.

### 18. Metabase, "Institutional Memory" — OPENED
URL: https://www.metabase.com/blog/institutional-memory  (Sameer Al-Sakran, Mar 14, 2016)
- "Institutional memory is a company's collective knowledge of what things mean, how they've changed, and who changed them."
- "Make sure that you document definitions of metrics, what they are meant to capture, how they are computed, and their historical changes. As they change, budget time to update any central documents."
- "If something is in your face every day, you're more likely to keep it up to date."
Relevance: memory = definitions + their change history + who changed them; kept current only if used daily (a consumer for the record).

## E. Product ops and the single source of truth

### 19. Productboard, "Why a single source of truth is critical for product roadmapping" — OPENED (vendor)
URL: https://www.productboard.com/blog/why-a-single-source-of-truth-is-critical-for-product-roadmapping/  (January 14, 2025)
- "A single source of truth (SSoT) in the context of product development refers to a centralized repository or framework where all information, decisions, and updates about a product are stored and managed."
- "Without a product single source of truth, teams often struggle with miscommunication, redundant work, and misaligned priorities."
- "An SSoT is only effective if it's trusted. What does that mean? It is always up-to-date and supported by data-driven decisions."
Search-only (UNOPENED): Dragonboat "Good Product Ops, Bad Product Ops" https://dragonboat.io/blog/good-product-ops-bad-product-ops/ and "Product Operations 101" https://dragonboat.io/blog/product-operations-101/ — snippet: product ops "evaluating, owning, and managing portfolio tooling to enable a single source of truth".

### 20. GitLab handbook — product processes, handbook-first, direction page — UNOPENED / ABSTRACT only
URLs tried: https://handbook.gitlab.com/handbook/product/product-processes/ (returned navigation only, twice); https://handbook.gitlab.com/handbook/company/culture/all-remote/handbook-first/ (navigation only, direct and via r.jina.ai); https://handbook.gitlab.com/handbook/values/ (navigation only); https://about.gitlab.com/direction/ (403 direct; via r.jina.ai only the "What's coming" block was readable: "Planned features across upcoming releases. Plans subject to change." with epic/issue links, current release "GitLab 19.3", August 20, 2026).
Nothing further quotable; GitLab's decision practices could not be verified from the handbook text this session. Recorded as unopened.

### 21. Notion product-management templates — UNOPENED (404 on the category URL tried: https://www.notion.com/templates/category/product-management)

## F. Wardley mapping for "where we are"

### 22. Simon Wardley, "On being lost" (Medium, wardleymaps, ch.1, 2016) — OPENED via r.jina.ai (direct fetch 403)
URL: https://medium.com/wardleymaps/on-being-lost-2ef5f05eb1ec
- "Situational awareness, use of terrain and maps appeared to be vital techniques in the outcome of any conflict."
- "If I was going to move a piece on a map then I could point to where it was and where it needed to go."
- Map elements: "Visual representation, context specific, position of components relative to some form of anchor and movement of those components".
- "Every single diagram I was using to determine strategy in business lacked one or more of those basic elements."
- "You learn from that context and how pieces move in it, in much the same way you learn from games in chess".
Relevance: Wardley's test for a "where we are" artifact — it must have an anchor (the user need), position, and movement; most product diagrams (and roadmaps) fail the movement/position test.

## Conflicts and gaps noted
- Direction artifact: all roadmap authors opened (Bastow, Cagan, Perri, McCarthy-secondhand) agree the unit is a problem/outcome/theme, not a feature, and that dates are avoided; Cagan goes further and rejects the roadmap as an artifact in favour of vision + objectives, while Bastow/McCarthy keep a roadmap but re-typed. Linear keeps a dated "product timeline" ("slightly in front of you") — a mild conflict with the no-dates school.
- "Where we are": only Perri (current state / target condition), Bastow ("Now" column), Linear (initiative status + health), GitHub (preview/GA/retired tags) and Wardley (position on a map) give it an explicit artifact element; Cagan's vision/objectives do not.
- "Where we've been": carried by changelogs/release notes (keepachangelog, Stripe, GitHub, Linear, GitLab) and by decision records (Charak PDR, Productboard "product memory"). The two are different histories — what shipped vs why decided — and no opened source unifies them; Quackback claims the changelog is "an institutional record of product decisions", which the decision-record authors would dispute (a changelog records outputs, not rationale).
- Changelog ownership: GitLab names the PM as owner; keepachangelog is silent on ownership; Linear says changelog benefits "internal and external communication" but does not name an owner.
- "Changelog as product memory" as a named practitioner idea: only a vendor guide (Quackback) and a vendor "product memory" piece (Productboard) found; no independent practitioner essay located — confidence low-medium on that phrase as a recognised practice.
- GitLab handbook decision practices: not verifiable this session (pages served navigation only); anything about GitLab decisions beyond the release-notes page is unopened.

1	# Notes-3 — SQ3: features crossing Bounded Contexts; product-level requests → context-owning teams
2	
3	Gathered 2026-08-26 via WebFetch/WebSearch. Status per source: **opened in full** (tool returned page body and quotes were checked against it), **partial** (tool returned extracted quotes only; page body not seen whole), **could not be opened**. Quotes are verbatim as returned by the fetch tool; where the tool paraphrased I say so and do not quote. Nothing below is from memory.
4	
5	---
6	
7	## A. DDD sources
8	
9	### A1. Evans, *DDD Reference* (2015) — https://www.domainlanguage.com/wp-content/uploads/2016/05/DDD_Reference_2015-03.pdf
10	Status: **partial** (direct fetch 403; opened via r.jina.ai, pattern text returned verbatim).
11	- Bounded Context: "Explicitly define the context within which a model applies. Explicitly set boundaries in terms of team organization, usage within specific parts of the application, and physical manifestations such as code bases and database schemas."
12	- Context Map: "Identify each model in play on the project and define its bounded context. Name each bounded context, and make the names part of the ubiquitous language. Describe the points of contact between the models, outlining explicit translation for any communication."
13	- Partnership: "Where development failure in either of two contexts would result in delivery failure for both, forge a partnership between the teams in charge of the two contexts. Institute a process for coordinated planning of development and joint management of integration."
14	- Customer/Supplier Development: "Establish a clear customer/supplier relationship between the two teams, meaning downstream priorities factor into upstream planning. Negotiate and budget tasks for downstream requirements so that everyone understands the commitment and schedule."
15	- Conformist: "Eliminate the complexity of translation between bounded contexts by slavishly adhering to the model of the upstream team."
16	- Anticorruption Layer: "As a downstream client, create an isolating layer to provide your system with functionality of the upstream system in terms of your own domain model."
17	- Open-host Service: "Define a protocol that gives access to your subsystem as a set of services. Open the protocol so that all who need to integrate with you can use it. Enhance and expand the protocol to handle new integration requirements."
18	- Published Language: "Use a well-documented shared language that can express the necessary domain information as a common medium of communication, translating as necessary into and out of that language."
19	- Separate Ways: "Declare a bounded context to have no connection to the others at all, allowing developers to find simple, specialized solutions within this small scope."
20	- Big Ball of Mud: "Draw a boundary around the entire mess and designate it a big ball of mud. Do not try to apply sophisticated modeling within this context."
21	Relevance: Evans' unit for cross-context work is the *relationship between the two teams* (Partnership / Customer-Supplier), planned and budgeted as such — not a feature artifact. A feature spanning contexts is handled as coordinated planning under a named context-map relationship. No "feature" pattern exists in the Reference.
22	
23	### A2. Fowler, bliki "BoundedContext" (2014) — https://martinfowler.com/bliki/BoundedContext.html
24	Status: **opened in full**.
25	- "Bounded Context is a central pattern in Domain-Driven Design."
26	- "total unification of the domain model for a large system will not be feasible or cost-effective"
27	- "Bounded Contexts have both unrelated concepts (such as a support ticket only existing in a customer support context) but also share concepts (such as products and customers)."
28	- "Different contexts may have completely different models of common concepts with mechanisms to map between these polysemic concepts for integration."
29	- "Usually the dominant one is human culture, since models act as Ubiquitous Language, you need a different model when the language changes."
30	- "DDD's strategic design goes on to describe a variety of ways that you have relationships between Bounded Contexts. It's usually worthwhile to depict these using a context map."
31	Relevance: contexts are partitions of *model and team*, not of features; shared concepts (customer, product) appear in several contexts by design, so a product-level feature touching "customer" will necessarily touch several.
32	
33	### A3. Vernon, InfoQ report "Microservices and DDD" (2016) — https://www.infoq.com/news/2016/07/microservices-ddd-vernon
34	Status: **partial** (extracted quotes; secondhand report of Vernon's talk/writing).
35	- "one service per bounded context"; "one service and one bounded context should be one deployable unit"
36	- "modelling microservices in a bounded context determined in size by the ubiquitous language"
37	- "publishing the events for eventual use of other microservices"
38	- "With experience though, they may become more fine granular, creating more microservices and deployable units"
39	Relevance: cross-context coordination is via published domain events; the context, not the feature, is the deployable/owned unit.
40	
41	### A4. Vernon, *IDDD* ch.14 (O'Reilly excerpt) — https://www.oreilly.com/library/view/implementing-domain-driven-design/9780133039900/ch14lev1sec2.html
42	Status: **could not be opened** (403 direct and via r.jina.ai). Not cited.
43	
44	### A5. Microsoft p&p, *CQRS Journey* "Reference 6: A Saga on Sagas" (2012–14) — https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/previous-versions/msp-n-p/jj591569(v=pandp.10)
45	Status: **opened in full**.
46	- "The term saga is commonly used in discussions of CQRS to refer to a piece of code that coordinates and routes messages between bounded contexts and aggregates. However, for the purposes of this guidance we prefer to use the term process manager to refer to this type of code artifact."
47	- "Typically, commands are sent within a bounded context. Events may have subscribers in the same bounded context as where they are published, or in other bounded contexts."
48	- "In a complex system that you have modeled using aggregates and bounded contexts, there may be some business processes that involve multiple aggregates, or multiple aggregates in multiple bounded contexts. In these business processes multiple messages of different types are exchanged by the participating aggregates."
49	- "Secondly, the definition of the message flow is now located in a single place, the process manager, rather than being scattered throughout the aggregates."
50	- "It's important to note that the process manager does not perform any business logic. It only routes messages, and in some cases translates between message types."
51	- "Typically, you would expect to see a process manager routing messages between aggregates within a bounded context, and you would expect to see a saga managing a long-running business process that spans multiple bounded contexts."
52	Relevance: the technical answer to "a feature crosses contexts" is a named cross-context *process* (saga) with the flow defined in one place; each context still owns its own logic. This is the code-level analogue of a product-level artifact that names the whole flow and points to the contexts it touches.
53

205	## Distilled findings for SQ3
206	
207	1. **No DDD source has a "feature" artifact.** Evans' units are context, context map, and *relationship between teams* (Partnership, Customer/Supplier, etc.). A feature spanning contexts is handled by coordinated planning under a named relationship (A1). Confidence: high (primary opened).
208	2. **Cross-context flow is a first-class code artifact** — saga/process manager holding the flow "in a single place" while contexts keep their logic (A5; A3 for events). Confidence: high for the CQRS-Journey text; Vernon's own text unopened (medium for attribution to him).

210	4. **Modern org practice maps context → team** (Plöd/INNOQ, TT+DDD minibook, Vernon) and then handles cross-team features by **named interaction modes** (TT B1) or by **initiatives with a champion, prioritised above teams, capped at ~1/3 capacity** (Fowler/Narayan B4). 211	5. **Contrast — LeSS**: one product backlog, feature teams, items not pre-assigned; context-owning teams are "component teams" with dependency/waterfall drawbacks (B8, B9). Direct conflict with the DDD/TT position; TT's stream-aligned team (aligned to journey/persona, no hand-offs, B3) sits between the two.
212	6. **Frequency of cross-context features is the diagnostic.** Newman: wrong boundaries → "larger number of cross-service changes" → merge back (B7); Tune: "corresponding changes between one or more systems… serious warning signs" (A9). Implies the process should *count* cross-context features and feed the count back to the architect (ties to `feedback-loops-with-consumers`).
213	7. **Recurring cross-capability flows can be re-homed** as their own owned thing (Fowler B5: checkout "might need a team of their own"). Confidence: medium.
214	8. **Failure mode documented**: autonomous teams with no defined cross-team feature process (Spotify, B10). Confidence: medium (one practitioner account).
215	
216	Conflicts to carry: (a) LeSS "feature team owns the whole feature" vs DDD/TT "context/stream team owns the slice, coordinate the rest"; (b) TT stream = journey/product (feature rarely crosses) vs Plöd "bounded contexts are the preferred way of identifying boundaries for teams" (feature often crosses) — both under the TT banner.
217	
218	Gap relative to our process: the industry answer to "request against a product, feature across contexts" is a product-level artifact **above** the context brief (initiative / saga-flow / journey) with a named owner, plus a measured signal of how often it is needed. Nothing opened supports making the per-context brief the first artifact.

## A. DDD sources

### A1. Evans, *DDD Reference* (2015) — https://www.domainlanguage.com/wp-content/uploads/2016/05/DDD_Reference_2015-03.pdf
Status: **partial** (direct fetch 403; opened via r.jina.ai, pattern text returned verbatim).
- Bounded Context: "Explicitly define the context within which a model applies. Explicitly set boundaries in terms of team organization, usage within specific parts of the application, and physical manifestations such as code bases and database schemas."
- Context Map: "Identify each model in play on the project and define its bounded context. Name each bounded context, and make the names part of the ubiquitous language. Describe the points of contact between the models, outlining explicit translation for any communication."
- Partnership: "Where development failure in either of two contexts would result in delivery failure for both, forge a partnership between the teams in charge of the two contexts. Institute a process for coordinated planning of development and joint management of integration."
- Customer/Supplier Development: "Establish a clear customer/supplier relationship between the two teams, meaning downstream priorities factor into upstream planning. Negotiate and budget tasks for downstream requirements so that everyone understands the commitment and schedule."
- Conformist: "Eliminate the complexity of translation between bounded contexts by slavishly adhering to the model of the upstream team."
- Anticorruption Layer: "As a downstream client, create an isolating layer to provide your system with functionality of the upstream system in terms of your own domain model."
- Open-host Service: "Define a protocol that gives access to your subsystem as a set of services. Open the protocol so that all who need to integrate with you can use it. Enhance and expand the protocol to handle new integration requirements."
- Published Language: "Use a well-documented shared language that can express the necessary domain information as a common medium of communication, translating as necessary into and out of that language."
- Separate Ways: "Declare a bounded context to have no connection to the others at all, allowing developers to find simple, specialized solutions within this small scope."
- Big Ball of Mud: "Draw a boundary around the entire mess and designate it a big ball of mud. Do not try to apply sophisticated modeling within this context."
Relevance: Evans' unit for cross-context work is the *relationship between the two teams* (Partnership / Customer-Supplier), planned and budgeted as such — not a feature artifact. ## Distilled findings for SQ3

1. **No DDD source has a "feature" artifact.** Evans' units are context, context map, and *relationship between teams* (Partnership, Customer/Supplier, etc.). A feature spanning contexts is handled by coordinated planning under a named relationship (A1). Confidence: high (primary opened).
2. **Cross-context flow is a first-class code artifact** — saga/process manager holding the flow "in a single place" while contexts keep their logic (A5; A3 for events). Confidence: high for the CQRS-Journey text; Vernon's own text unopened (medium for attribution to him).
3. **Product-level composites are not contexts.** Tune: dashboards and journeys are "a composite of capabilities provided by other bounded contexts"; journey changes force "multiple business capability teams" to coordinate — by design (A8, A9). Confidence: medium (one author, two posts).
4. **Modern org practice maps context → team** (Plöd/INNOQ, TT+DDD minibook, Vernon) and then handles cross-team features by **named interaction modes** (TT B1) or by **initiatives with a champion, prioritised above teams, capped at ~1/3 capacity** (Fowler/Narayan B4). Confidence: high for B4 (opened in full); medium for the mapping claim.
5. **Contrast — LeSS**: one product backlog, feature teams, items not pre-assigned; context-owning teams are "component teams" with dependency/waterfall drawbacks (B8, B9). Direct conflict with the DDD/TT position; TT's stream-aligned team (aligned to journey/persona, no hand-offs, B3) sits between the two.
6. **Frequency of cross-context features is the diagnostic.** Newman: wrong boundaries → "larger number of cross-service changes" → merge back (B7); Tune: "corresponding changes between one or more systems… serious warning signs" (A9). Implies the process should *count* cross-context features and feed the count back to the architect (ties to `feedback-loops-with-consumers`).
7. **Recurring cross-capability flows can be re-homed** as their own owned thing (Fowler B5: checkout "might need a team of their own"). Confidence: medium.
8. **Failure mode documented**: autonomous teams with no defined cross-team feature process (Spotify, B10). Confidence: medium (one practitioner account).

Conflicts to carry: (a) LeSS "feature team owns the whole feature" vs DDD/TT "context/stream team owns the slice, coordinate the rest"; (b) TT stream = journey/product (feature rarely crosses) vs Plöd "bounded contexts are the preferred way of identifying boundaries for teams" (feature often crosses) — both under the TT banner.

Gap relative to our process: the industry answer to "request against a product, feature across contexts" is a product-level artifact **above** the context brief (initiative / saga-flow / journey) with a named owner, plus a measured signal of how often it is needed. Nothing opened supports making the per-context brief the first artifact.

# Product Strategy: Vision Over Plan

According to Melissa Perri's article, effective product strategy differs fundamentally from traditional planning. She argues that organizations often conflate these concepts, mistakenly treating strategy as a feature roadmap.

## Core Components

Perri identifies four essential elements:

**Vision** represents the long-term directional goal for the company or business unit.

**Challenge** serves as "the first Business goal you have to achieve on the way to your longer term vision," functioning as a strategic objective that focuses teams on specific product development areas.

**Target Condition** functions to break down the broader challenge. "These are set in terms of achievable, measurable metrics." Critically, "It should be measured and quantified before the work starts to achieve the first target condition."

**Current State** establishes baseline measurements against which progress is tracked.

## Key Insight

The fundamental distinction Perri emphasizes is that product strategy should emerge through experimentation toward measurable business objectives, not through predetermined feature lists. This approach aligns teams around outcomes rather than outputs, enabling flexibility in response to market learning while maintaining strategic coherence.

# The Alternative to Roadmaps: Key Concepts

Based on Marty Cagan's article, here are the essential principles:

## Core Vision Components

**The Product Vision:** "this describes the holistic view of what the organization as a whole is trying to accomplish."

**The Business Objectives:** "this describes the specific, prioritized business objectives for each product team."

## Measuring Success

The fundamental shift involves recognizing that "It is all about outcome rather than output." Rather than tracking completed features, teams focus on whether solutions actually achieve their intended business results.

## Managing Commitments

When specific date-based or deliverable commitments are necessary, the approach uses what Cagan terms "high-integrity commitments"—ensuring accountability through transparent, realistic promises rather than feature-based roadmap items.

## The Transformation

By providing clear context through vision and objectives while empowering teams to determine solutions, organizations move from command-and-control management toward autonomous teams that take ownership of business outcomes. This approach addresses the two traditional roadmap purposes—prioritization and accountability—through a more outcome-focused framework.

# Intercom's Product Roadmap Approach

## The Intermission Document

Intercom uses a quirky naming convention for their project briefs. As they explain: "The Intermission is our quirky name for a project brief. This document is the responsibility of the Product Manager. It is restricted to less than one page and must succinctly cover the problem we're solving, how we will measure success, and the scope of the project. It never includes solutions because this comes later."

The key principle here is that these briefs focus on problem definition rather than proposing answers.

## Roadmap Structure

The company organizes their planning hierarchically. According to their process: "Everything in our roadmap is broken down by team objective, which is broken down into multiple projects, which in turn are broken down into individual releases."

This tiered approach allows Intercom to maintain strategic alignment while enabling rapid execution through smaller, manageable increments.
